speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: This Motion represents the voices of our leaders and workers discussing AI transition in the last two years or so.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: I want to speak today: to the young graduates wondering if their skills will be enough; to the mid-career professionals asking whether their experience still counts; to the blue-collar workers worried if they will have good jobs in an AI-enabled economy.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: Today, in an AI-enabled world, we must renew that compact, deliberately and together.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: It is reshaping how work is done, how we serve customers and how value is created.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: Consulting firms, such as KPMG and Accenture, are starting to include the use of AI to achieve business outcomes as a staff assessment.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: More recently, leading technology firms, like Meta and Microsoft, have announced global restructuring plans.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: AI may not be the only driver of these changes.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: But they show clearly that the nature of work is changing fast.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: AI is impacting junior roles, which were once the first rung of a career ladder.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: Across the economy, AI is reducing the need for junior staff to spend long hours on data processing and standardised modelling.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: AI is also reshaping professional, manager and executive (PME) jobs in higher-end professions, like doctors, lawyers and accountants.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: At the same time, AI is also creating new jobs, new roles.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: But even as new opportunities emerge, workers have real and understandable concerns.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: Young graduates ask: where do I start, and how do I build the right skills when the first rung is now higher?

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: Many mid-career PMEs and workers ask: will my experience count?

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: How can AI strengthen my role and not replace me?

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: Taken together, these shifts challenge the assumption that economic growth will always lead to more and better jobs.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: Our economic agencies continue to bring in good investments.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: The Government has set out clear ambitions to strengthen an AI-enabled economy.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: But for many Singaporeans on the ground, two questions remain: how can I take part in this growth and benefit from it?

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: How will this growth translate into fair opportunities for me?

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: Around the world, we can see the extremes of what happens when these questions are left unanswered.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: On one extreme, some societies allow technology to race ahead.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: Displaced workers are left to fend for themselves.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: Economists warn of scars when job disruption is unmanaged.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: In Hollywood, writers and actors have taken to picket lines and public demonstrations over the use of AI.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: These are not paths that we want for Singapore.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: This is why today, my fellow Parliamentarians and I put forward this Motion to set out a clear agenda for AI adoption, one that strengthens Singapore's competitiveness, supports our enterprises and empowers our workers.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: We must build on our tripartite strengths for this new AI-enabled era to ensure that it benefits all workers.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: To that end, Mr Mark Lee will address the clarity for enterprises, our AI front door; Mr Saktiandi Supaat will speak on building an inclusive AI-enabled economy for Singapore; and Ms Yeo Wan Ling will speak on job redesign for the future of work.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: AI is advancing at such speed that even its creators are acknowledging its limits and the need for guardrails, safeguards.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: In fact, AI has widened the scope of what one person can do quite incredibly.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: In many countries, "solopreneuers", or one-person outfits, are using AI to carry out work previously done by whole teams.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: It is reshaping business models and organisational structures.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: Against this backdrop, the concerns raised to the Labour Movement are grounded in lived experience.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: Workers worry their skills may not keep pace.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: Many want to transform but are weighing workforce readiness and implementation costs.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: NTUC is also seeing more than double the number of enterprises seeking support on AI-related projects and asking how to seize new opportunities.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: We must strengthen our plans and responses at this stage of the AI-enabled growth, before disruption takes hold.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: This is the proactive AI future we must work towards because our people are our greatest strength.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: I am sure that everyone in this House agrees.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: Used well, it can raise productivity, unlock new possibilities and strengthen our competitiveness.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: But every worker, who puts in the fair share of effort must be able to see where they can fit into this new economy and be supported to get there.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: This is how we anchor AI-enabled growth in fairness, resilience and opportunity for all.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: Singapore has never waited for disruption to hit before acting.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: We have always chosen to look ahead and prepare early.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: When technology reshaped work in the past, tripartite partners stepped up together: during the National Computerisation Plan in the 1980s; through the Skills Programme for Upgrading and Resilience during the Global Financial Crisis; and through the NTUC Job Security Council during COVID-19, which helped thousands of workers displaced overnight to return to work.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: At Budget, our Government underscored the need to support workers and companies to adapt and succeed in an AI-enabled economy, with the Prime Minister chairing the National AI Council.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: What matters now is how we take this tripartite commitment to act early and act together, with a humble approach that keeps us close to the ground, so that our AI ambitions translate into confidence and opportunities for enterprises and most importantly, Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: First, we must build market intelligence and foresight for an AI-enabled economy.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: In this period of rapid change, workers and enterprises do not just need more information.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: They need trusted intelligence, grounded in Singapore's own labour market realities.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: Today, workers and enterprises face a fragmented, sometimes even conflicting, view of the AI landscape.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: Some global reports warn of large-scale job displacement.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: Others say that AI is the future of white-collar work.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: The landing point is fuzzy and still uncertain.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: That is why Singapore needs our own trusted system of market intelligence and foresight, one that reflects our sectoral mix, workforce profile and enterprise realities.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: Workers, both white and blue collars alike, need practical answers and guidance: which roles are evolving?

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: For youths, this could mean clearer signals on which skills will open doors so that training pathways can be better designed to match labour demand.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: It also means a less anxious transition from school to work, even as entry level roles change.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: For PMEs and blue-collar workers, this means early guidance on how to upskill, use AI to augment their roles, expand their job scope and improve work prospects.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: With targeted reskilling, workers can raise their value and move confidently into new, redesigned or adjacent roles.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: Good research can also help us avoid reactive policy-making because intervening only after displacement has occurred is far more costly, financially, economically and socially.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: By reskilling workers before their roles diminish, they are also far more likely to stay employed and progress.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: This is why a market intelligence and foresight system, tailored to Singapore, matters.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: It brings together insights from trade associations on how industries are adopting AI, enterprise data on job redesign and productivity shifts, and union sensing on worker concerns, skills stress points and what upskilling is actually working.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: This is foresight and intelligence that Singaporeans can trust because it combines macro data on the one hand and ground realities on the other, from unions who know their workers, as well from employers navigating AI transformation.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: With such a system, tripartite partners can better make sense of how work is evolving.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: Enterprises and workers will not be left guessing.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: They will have clearer direction, more time to prepare and better support to move into new opportunities.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: Second, we must enable enterprises to transform with AI and do so in a way that benefits workers.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: Enterprises must be empowered to adopt AI, with workers actively involved so that transformation delivers stronger business performance and better workforce outcomes.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: We can already see some possibilities of what can happen when AI adoption is intentional, phased and paired with workforce upgrading.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: At ST Engineering Land Systems, together with the ST Engineering Staff Union and the former SkillsFuture Singapore, workers across more than 40 suppliers are being trained in AI and new precision engineering tools to meet the evolving needs of advanced manufacturing.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: Supporting more SMEs means more workers can benefit from AI-enabled transformation.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: Across enterprises large and small, we must ensure that training, job progression and wage outcomes are built into the transformation process from Day One.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: Worker outcomes must be part of the business transformation plans, not left to chance or treated as an afterthought.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: This is why NTUC pioneered the concept of the Company Training Committee, so that transformation uplifts businesses and workers together.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: We forged skills training, job redesign and clearer career development pathways together with transforming businesses.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: Tan Tock Seng Hospital and the Healthcare Services Employees' Union are tapping on the Company Training Committee to scale PreSAGE.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: This means nurses no longer need to go ward after ward, potentially across 1,200 beds, to manually check where the fall sensor mats need to be placed.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: This new workflow is faster and smarter and less demanding.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: It designs out tedious, repetitive, labour-intensive work and it makes, in this case, nursing more sustainable and meaningful, especially also for the older staff.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: We are also partnering GP+ Co-operative to support general practitioners (GPs) to use AI, to upskill clinic staff on case documentation and raise overall productivity.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: In this case, NTUC and our unions stand with GP doctors, not only as healthcare professionals but also as small business owners navigating change.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: The Company Training Committee works because it is built on a win-win foundation – enterprises transform and workers progress with them.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: Up to now, the Labour Movement has spearheaded the Company Training Committee initiative.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: Going forward, I propose that we do so together with the Singapore National Employers Federation (SNEF) as part of the new Tripartite Jobs Council.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: In other words, both NTUC and SNEF will work together to expand and scale the Company Training Committees nation-wide.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: Together, with our networks, we can reach more enterprises and more workers.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: We can provide more focused AI-related support and achieve more win-win outcomes.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: And in that process, Minister Tan See Leng is just walking back into the Chamber, we will likely need more resources for this new Company Training Committee implementation approach.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: NTUC will work through the details with SNEF and put up our requests for funding when ready, and we hope the Government will provide its full support.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: As AI reshapes industries and business models, the impact on jobs will continue to evolve.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: For our youths and our workers, having clearer signals, better pathways and practical support can help them move into new opportunities.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: Through the Tripartite Jobs Council, we should strengthen our outreach to IHLs so that students can gain labour-market insights and plan their career moves earlier during their studies.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: We can do more as an ecosystem to help our youths make informed choices and shorten the transition from school to work.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: I met several young professionals recently when I visited Amazon Web Services (AWS).

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: Some of these fresh graduates had initial anxieties but ultimately managed to secure positions after a period of job searches.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: Ending up in AWS is a good outcome.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: But it raised a question in my mind too.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: Could the journey have been smoother with earlier career guidance, better insight into employer needs and stronger matching for internships and entry-level roles?

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: NTUC's e2i has developed an AI Career Coach to help youths and jobseekers improve their resumes, practise mock job interviews and receive feedback for improvement.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: Through tailored job suggestions, youths can get a boost to help with their job searches and perhaps, make the process that little bit less daunting.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: For PMEs and mid-career workers, the challenge is different – 56% of PMEs surveyed by NTUC felt that they need to upskill to keep pace with AI.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: Our PMEs will need confidence that skills upgrading can translate into real job opportunities and that their experience will continue to matter.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: To address the needs, NTUC LearningHub has developed AI skills pathways at different levels of proficiency.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: Our unions will do their part as well.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: The Union Training Assistance Programme will be expanded to help offset the cost of subscriptions to selected AI tools.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: Our unions will also work closely with sectoral champions to ensure that AI training for our workers is practical and support their daily work.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: Sector by sector, company by company, we will help enterprises and workers utilise the Company Training Committee to transform their business processes and operating models to reap the benefits of AI.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: Today, there is strong demand for digital transformation and AI-related Company Training Committee projects.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: I visited SIN(G) Assurance PAC earlier this year, a public accounting firm that offers audit and assurance services.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: Journal entry testing used to involve long hours of repetitive scanning and junior auditors depended heavily on managers for technical guidance.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: Using the Company Training Committee grant, the firm implemented a quality management tool that eliminated tedious and time-consuming manual tracking of spreadsheets.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: It also adopted robotic process automation and deployed an AI-enabled chatbot to improve audit efficiency and accuracy.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: Technology is now a force multiplier for SMEs like SIN(G) Assurance PAC.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: It enables workers to apply their professional judgement to higher-value work.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: Cases like these show us that when transformation is done with workers at the centre, enterprises and workers both benefit.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: We will bring these capabilities to the Tripartite Jobs Council, so that we can pool resources and make it easier for workers of all collars to seize new opportunities as AI reshapes work.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: Fourth, we must enable displaced workers to bounce back with dignity and confidence.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: The impact of AI on jobs will continue to evolve.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: We must keep a vigilant watch on emerging AI governance issues and adapt our policies, even our laws.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: Keeping human-in-the-loop will be important, especially in areas like hiring, work allocation, performance management and dismissal decisions.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: But even with these best efforts, we must be honest that some displacement will still occur, particularly among the PMEs.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: In the age where AI displacement may be more pronounced, we must find ways to reach affected workers early and shorten the time between disruption and recovery.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: For displaced workers who have put in years of hard work, retrenchment can feel sudden and deeply unsettling, as if the ground has shifted from beneath them.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: This should be done before the employee's last working day.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: I am glad that this is being studied in the ongoing review of the Employment Act.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: The purpose is to help affected workers adapt and bounce back as quickly as possible while keeping our labour market flexible and dynamic.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: In practice, especially for larger-scale retrenchments, earlier notice allows our unions, allows e2i, through its network of 27 National Career Centres, to come in early to support affected workers.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: I am heartened that many companies undergoing restructuring already provide such early notification.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: This has allowed tripartite partners to deploy career and emotional support onsite.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: In such cases, we were able to offer immediate reskilling pathways and work directly with employers to line up suitable vacancies, sometimes even before the affected workers' last day of work.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: Beyond job matching, displaced workers must be supported to bounce back too with dignity, with real opportunities to train, transit and move to the next good job.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: Mr Hong, a mid-career IT manager in the retail industry, was retrenched when his company offshored its IT support.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: Despite 15 years of experience managing enterprise IT systems, his opportunities were limited.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: He felt dejected, lost and unsure where to restart.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: Thankfully, with career guidance and coaching from NTUC's e2i, Mr Hong was able to pivot to the healthcare industry as an IT manager within a short time.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: Like Mr Hong, many workers feel vulnerable after retrenchment, especially after years of contribution to the same organisation.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: For those with a mortgage, with school-going children or with ageing parents to support, the pressure to find a job quickly is very real.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: It provides time-bound support, tied to active job searches and training.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: Today, this JSS is pegged to a median income of about $5,000.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: But in the AI era, many PMEs earning above this level may face the same displacement risks and the same need for structured transition support.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: Adjusting coverage closer to the PME median gross income levels would better reflect the realities of the AI-driven disruption.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: Our aim is not to preserve old jobs.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: It is to help Singaporeans move, over time, more confidently into the next good job faster.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: Together with earlier notification, quicker and more coordinated mobilisation, we can ensure that displaced workers recover faster and bounce back with confidence.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: (In Mandarin): In this AI era, countries are transforming rapidly, businesses are adapting and jobs are changing.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: Young people are asking, "What should I study to go further in my career?" Workers are also asking, "How can my experience continue to add value in this age of AI?" Therefore, we must act early.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: We must integrate business transformation with worker training to ensure that economic growth translates into quality jobs for our workers.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: NTUC will work with institutes of higher learning to strengthen career coaching and career planning, so that graduating youths are able to find suitable jobs more quickly.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: At the same time, we propose for local businesses, unions and academia to jointly study the impact of AI on employment.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: Through NTUC's Company Training Committee Grant, we will strengthen support for businesses to adopt AI and seize new opportunities.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: In doing so, white collar workers will be able to harness AI and take on higher value work.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: Blue collar workers will also be able to upgrade their AI skills and access new growth pathways.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: For those who need to switch careers, we will walk alongside them as they make a fresh start.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: I began this speech with the questions on many workers' minds: how can I take part in the AI growth and benefit from it?

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: How can I translate into fair opportunities for me?

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: As we enter the next phase of growth, we must review our steadfast commitment to support our workers.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: Young graduates, white collar PMEs, younger or older, blue collar workers alike.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: Enable workers to seize new opportunities as jobs evolve.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: The question is as moved by Mr Ng Chee Meng.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: You need to move that the debate be now adjourned.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: It must also be designed into the way enterprises transform, the way jobs are redesigned and the way our system supports firms to move with confidence.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: History shows that in periods of technological change, the winners are not those who try to protect existing business models but those who understand their underlying strengths well enough to redeploy them into new arenas.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: It did not survive the collapse of film by trying to sell more film.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: It built on capabilities in materials, optics and imaging to move into skincare, diagnostics and healthcare technology.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: In sectors where Singapore is already strong – advanced manufacturing, logistics and connectivity, finance and healthcare – AI is not replacing the industry itself but changing how value is created within the industry.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Our task is not to preserve every job exactly as it is.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Our task is to help our enterprises and our workforce recognise their strengths, adapt them and move into the next phase of growth together.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: I will divide my remarks into three parts: first, what AI is actually doing for businesses; second, its impact on jobs and workers; and third, how we can build a clearer enterprise front door and a wider bridge forward so that businesses and workers can cross the transition together.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Global evidence shows how AI adoption is increasingly concentrated among higher-skilled workers, with firms re-organising work around smaller, more experienced teams supported by AI.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: This creates a double risk: first, productivity gains may accrue more to those already ahead, widening inequality; second, it risks eroding the bottom of the career ladder.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: If entry-level roles are reduced too quickly, the traditional pathway where workers build judgement through experience is disrupted.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Firms may still require mid-level capability but fewer workers will have had the opportunity to develop it.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: At the same time, new roles are emerging, integrating AI into workflows, validating outputs, redesigning jobs and translating domain knowledge into solutions.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Companies like DBS and Mastercard are using AI to handle routine queries and personalise responses at scale, freeing up human agents for higher-value work.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: We are seeing the same among small and medium enterprises (SMEs).

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: MTM Labo, a skincare company, for example, uses an AI tool called Hana that supports customer enquiries in multiple languages, allowing its team to focus on more complex, high-touch interactions.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: AI, when deployed thoughtfully, does not just replace jobs.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: It changes the nature of jobs and can raise the value of human work.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: It requires integration into workflows, redesign of processes and alignment with business strategy.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: This is where many firms, especially SMEs, face challenges in translating AI into implementation.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: If we do not address this, capability will concentrate among larger firms and among more skilled workers.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: That outcome would run directly against the spirit of this Motion.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: However, we must also be careful about how we respond to these changes.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: I understand Mr Ng's good intent behind the call for earlier notification of retrenchment to better support workers.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: But if firms are not yet ready to redesign jobs or absorb workers differently, earlier notification alone will not solve the problem.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: If AI is re-organising work, perhaps a better solution that matters more is not whether we intervene earlier after displacement occurs but intervening early enough before displacement becomes necessary.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: We should shift the focus from managing retrenchment to enabling all firms to redesign jobs and retrain workers so that they transform and the workforce adjustment happens alongside transformation, not after it.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: This brings me to my third point – how do we we build a bridge forward?

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: A bridge that is wide enough for many to cross, not just a select few.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: But can we do more to help businesses?

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: This brings to my first dimension of practicality.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: One way forward is also for AI grants and schemes to have a more integrated approach where businesses can access this support through a single interface rather than navigating multiple agencies and deploy it flexibly, whether for basic implementation, subscriptions or experimentation, without repeated layers of claims, just like the SkillsFuture Enterprise Credit wallet.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: For larger or more complex customised projects, there may also be a case for more upfront support so that firms are not constrained by cashflow when making longer-term investments.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: At the same time, we must recognise that AI adoption involves experimentation.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: If firms are penalised despite genuine effort, we risk discouraging innovation.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: A reasonable tolerance for failure will be necessary if we want companies to move decisively.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: The pool of experienced AI professionals remains small and highly competitive.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: If we are too restrictive on bringing in foreign AI talents, we will slow down capability building across our economy.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: So, our efforts to build a wide bridge must also mean keeping our talent pipelines open.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Not just to bring in talent, but to allow that talent to cross-pollinate skills across firms and sectors.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: This can be time limited and on an application basis, with some checks in place to prevent abuse.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: The third dimension is through our institutes of higher learning (IHLs).

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: IHLs can be positioned more deliberately as execution platforms for applied AI, especially through Centres of Excellence anchored around postgraduate programmes.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Many postgraduate students, including foreign talent, bring prior industry experience and technical depth.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: When paired with local undergraduates, this creates a practical model for capability transfer.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: If anchored around real SME and sectoral problem statements, these teams can go beyond proof-of-concept work to develop deployable solutions.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: It lowers the cost of experimentation for SMEs while enabling cross-pollination between international and local talent, and it creates a pipeline for startups to emerge, anchored in Singapore and focused on solving real industry demands.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: This model also helps address to the broken career ladder.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: As entry-level pathways narrow, embedding students in real problem-solving builds capability earlier.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: At the same time, it strengthens our students' critical thinking, preparing them to question and validate AI and not just rely on it.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Today, many firms are attempting to solve similar AI problems in isolation.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: This leads to duplication of effort, higher experimentation costs and slower adoption.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Trade associations and chambers are structurally positioned to address this gap.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: They operate at the interface between government policy and firm-level behaviour and can translate national AI strategies into sector-specific implementation.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: They can function as coordinating platforms, identifying common industry problem statements, aggregating demand and working with solution providers and IHLs to develop integrated, deployable solutions aligned to actual workflows and job roles.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: SBF is developing an AI tool to help businesses understand the rules of origin of free trade agreements and how to apply preferential tariff treatment when goods are exported overseas.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: This is one example of how an industry‑led approach can reduce duplication and improve efficiency.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: For many SMEs, the challenge is also on applied capability.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Firms want to know which problems to prioritise, who can help and how to proceed without excessive cost or risk.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: It has been heavily oversubscribed because SMEs are looking for guided entry points.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: With the right support and funding, trade association and chambers can become platforms that accelerate AI adoption across sectors.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: The success of AI-enabled growth will not be determined by how many tools we deploy, but also by how many workers we carry through that change.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: I agree with Mr Ng that workers who are displaced, whether due to AI or industry consolidation, need stronger support during transition.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: But we should also consider how that support is structured.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Today, much of it follows a "train and place" approach, where workers are first retrained and then supported to find a job.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: This shortens the period of uncertainty for workers, while giving the firms the confidence to take in and develop new talent.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: This is also where trade associations and chambers, and unions can also play a coordinating role – identifying firms with demand and matching them with workers at risk.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Workers must see AI as enabling, not threatening.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: If AI is seen as a tool to remove jobs or close off pathways, adoption will slow not because the firms lack technology but because trust is lacking.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: And if that trust is broken, we may inadvertently create a lose-lose outcome where governments step in with more restricted workforce regulations around AI adoption, raising longer-term costs and reducing flexibility for businesses.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Only then can workers and businesses advance together.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I am also an advisor to the Union of Power and Gas Employees (UPAGE) and the Logistics and Supply Chain Union (SCEU).

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I will focus on how we can build a more inclusive AI economy, where growth is not only strong, but broadly shared.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: AI is no longer emerging; it is already reshaping how we work and live.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Beyond well-known AI tools, I saw this first-hand during engagements with the UPAGE, SCEU and, recently, Manpower Government Parliamentary Committee's learning journeys to SMRT, NTUC Finest at Punggol and Chye Thiam Maintenance Pte Ltd.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In different sectors, power and gas, supply chain, transport, retail, food and beverage (F&B), cleaning and facilities management, all of them embedding AI, autonomous vehicles (AVs) and robotics into workflows, raising productivity, creating new jobs and redesigning roles for existing workers.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: There is now a global race in AI innovation and adoption.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: And there is a growing belief that those economies and companies that move early and decisively will capture the greatest value.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: But Mr Speaker, Sir, as this House has consistently emphasised, economic success must be inclusive.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Economic success is not just growth, but how widely its benefits are shared.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Uneven growth is not a model Singapore should follow.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Besides the redistribution measures that we have implemented through tax measures and targeted assistance, we must cultivate a sustained mindset to ensure AI-enabled growth is inclusive.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Usage of AI has raised concerns for many workers.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: For example, will AI take away my job?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: For non-PMEs and lower-wage workers, the lower level of concern could be because they do not use AI tools as extensively and are unaware of how AI would impact their job opportunities and not because there is no AI-disruption risk.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: These concerns are reinforced by news of job restructuring globally, as well as uneven adoption of AI across sectors and occupations.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In banking here, AI is no longer emerging, it is already deeply embedded and a core driver of productivity.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Across the sector, our local banks are deploying automation in operations and customer servicing, particularly in labour-intensive and repeatable processes.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: These are not experimental use cases; they are transforming how work is done across the value chain.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: AI is now used in operations, such as processing, settlements and compliance, and in credit evaluation through machine learning models that support faster and more consistent underwriting.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It is even beginning — well, I would not say beginning; it is already playing a bigger role in hiring, particularly in initial screening.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: At the same time, regulation is sustaining demand for oversight roles in risk, compliance and audit.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: But crucially, more complex work still requires human judgement.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Handling nuanced customer issues, managing relationships and making judgement calls cannot be easily automated.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: As a result, many roles are not disappearing but evolving.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Our electricians, technicians and maintenance workers are essential.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: AI cannot repair lifts or maintain MRT systems on its own.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: As our economy becomes more digital, these roles will become more sophisticated, not less.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: If AI raises the premium on skills, we must also raise how we recognise mastery.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: But beyond recognition, we must also rethink how mastery is built.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: As AI reshapes how work is performed, we must also rethink how skills are transmitted.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Today, many of our industry transformation maps (ITMs) guide sectoral growth and workforce development.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: But they were largely designed for a pre-AI world.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: There may be merit in updating these frameworks to explicitly account for how AI is changing apprenticeship and on-the-job training pathways.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This issue has been raised in this House before and it deserves renewed attention.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: If we get this right, AI will not hollow out middle-skilled jobs, it will elevate them.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This will also help elevate further the skilled graduates from our Institutes of Technical Education (ITEs) and polytechnics.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Countries, such as the United Arab Emirates and Finland, have adopted coordinated national AI strategies combining government leadership, enterprise adoption and workforce development.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Here in Singapore, we have taken important steps.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: First, we must normalise AI as a way of life.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We must go beyond training pathways and time-limited access to AI tools.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: While I welcome the provision of temporary access through Government and NTUC initiatives, we must think ahead about what happens after this initial phase of subscriptions.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Many of the more capable AI tools require ongoing subscriptions.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Over time, this may create a divide between those who can afford to use these tools regularly and those who cannot.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: If left unaddressed, we risk creating a new form of inequality between AI "haves" and "have-nots".

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Because access to AI tools directly affects productivity, learning and income potential, unequal access will translate into unequal outcomes.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We should therefore consider how to ensure sustained and affordable access, especially for lower-income workers, freelancers, tradespersons and small businesses.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Possible approaches include a baseline level of subsidised access, similar to digital connectivity, tiered or group-based pricing with industry partners, shared access through community centres, libraries and training hubs, and ensuring employers receiving AI support also extend access to workers.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: And in the digital age, access to AI may become as fundamental as access to the Internet.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We must ensure no Singaporean is priced out of that future.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: One way to drive adoption is for the Government to be the "first customer" of useful AI tools and to mitigate AI transition-related concerns.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: AI-enabled systems can provide faster and more practical responses to citizens navigating Government services.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: As AI systems consistently deliver useful outcomes and quick advice to Singaporeans, confidence in AI and AI adoption will grow.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Against this backdrop, I would also like to acknowledge the Government's efforts to support workers through an AI-shaped economy, with employment remaining the central outcome and address job anxieties.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: As such, it is important to recognise, for example, that employment outcomes for the Malay/Muslim community under M³ and Focus Area 4 (FA4) have been delivered at both scale and through targeted support.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This reflects both the breadth of our national employment system and the depth of our community-anchored interventions.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Building on this, FA4 workstreams will sharpen their focus on supporting workers through an AI-shaped economy, with employment remaining the central outcome.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I am glad that NTUC will work closely with MENDAKI through NTUC's e2i to strengthen job transitions, particularly for young adults transiting from campus to career, who may be entering the workforce amid heightened uncertainty about job relevance and AI-driven displacement.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This includes strengthening early career pathways by partnering IHLs and integrating engagements with e2i's career services, job matching and employer networks, so that fresh graduates are better prepared for a changing labour market.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Taken together, these deliberate employment-linked interventions will help to ensure that productivity gains from AI do not result in jobless growth, but instead, equip Singaporeans, across life stages, to adapt, remain employable and progress with confidence, supported by NTUC, its partners and the wider Labour Movement.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: So, I encourage our community to take advantage of these initiatives to upskill.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Second, we must focus on the infrastructure that enables AI.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Systems, such as Singpass, already allow secure transactions, including legally binding processes, such as the Lasting Power of Attorney.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The next step is to enhance interoperability through application programming interfaces (APIs), so more services can be integrated seamlessly.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: When services are integrated, AI can significantly enhance efficiency and user experience.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: At the same time, we must calibrate data-sharing frameworks and safe harbours, so that data can be used responsibly without stifling innovation.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Third, we must ensure employers redesign workflows to embed AI meaningfully.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: While the Enterprise Workforce Transformation Package provides useful support, it tends to reach large firms that are already inclined to transform.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: While it can be on a voluntary "opt in" basis, like BCA's Green Mark Certification Scheme or TAFEP's Fair Employment Badge, the accreditation can be tied to certain other benefits or quotas to incentivise companies to come forward.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Like existing voluntary schemes, this could be linked to incentives to encourage broader participation.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Fourth, we must support those with traditional employers, tradesmen, lower-wage workers and platform workers.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: AI can act as a personal assistant, enhancing productivity and income.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Is there scope for the Government to invest in such tools and provide time-limited access, so these workers can experience their practical benefits?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Time constraints, caregiving responsibilities and life-stage challenges affect participation in training.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We should move forward towards flexible learning; integrate training into work; and strengthen cross-sector mobility.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This ensures our workforce remains agile, mobile and inclusive.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Through my interactions with Malay/Muslim workers, many see AI as an opportunity, but also worry that they cannot keep pace with this rapid technological advancement.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: PMETs in particular are beginning to ask: are my skills still relevant?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The fundamental question is: Does this AI economy have a place for me, or will I be left behind?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: As co-chair of the Economic Resilience Committee alongside Dr Wan Rizal, our focus is clear – to build and strengthen the economic resilience of our community by embracing the AI transition with openness and readiness.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: At the same time, we are developing targeted strategies to strengthen community involvement in economic transformation initiatives, so that participation can be deepened across all segments – from youth to professionals and entrepreneurs.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Within the Malay/Muslim community, this work has already begun and must be strengthened through the M³, now known as M³+.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Allow me to share some examples of efforts being undertaken by Malay/Muslim institutions to raise AI literacy among our community.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: At Majlis Ugama Islam Singapura (MUIS) (or Islamic Religious Council of Singapore) and the mosques, AI literacy programmes help the community understand the responsible use of technology.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The IftaSG initiative uses AI for Fatwa research.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Programmes encouraging thoughtful AI integration have also been made available to asatizah, to enable richer and more meaningful Islamic learning experiences.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: At Persatuan Ulama dan Guru-Guru Agama Islam Singapura (PERGAS), AI training equips asatizah with digital skills through programmes such as Diversity-driven Upskilling for Asatizah, the AI Accelerator Challenge, and AI for Asatizah Entrepreneurs.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: At the Association of Muslim Professionals, for working professionals, the "Learning Circles: All About GenAI" programme will be held this month.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It will explore how generative AI is reshaping the way we work and how professionals can begin applying it meaningfully in their daily roles.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This reflects a commitment to ensuring that technological progress serves as a catalyst for social mobility and inclusive growth within our community.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Mr Abdul Kadir bin Abdul Rahman, a veteran educator in science and mathematics, is a fine example of how three decades of deep experience can be combined with present-day innovation.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Now a trainer in the MAP programme, he is a strong advocate for using AI technology to improve learning quality.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: He has noted that one significant change is students' increased willingness to ask questions – fostering a more interactive and supportive learning environment.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: MENDAKI has partnered with institutions, such as SUTD, opening up opportunities in AI, design and application-based learning – so that our community is not merely a consumer of technology, but capable of mastering it.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This shows that AI can be a catalyst for social mobility – if we ensure that access and opportunity are widely shared.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: But not everyone starts from the same point.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Some have access, a supportive environment and the time to learn.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Others face constraints – whether in terms of time, family responsibilities, or self-confidence.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: That is why our approach must be inclusive.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Training must be accessible, relevant and practical, so that every individual has the opportunity to adapt and progress alongside these changes.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Ultimately, success in the AI economy is not measured by technology alone, but by how well we ensure that every citizen can move forward with confidence and hope. : Mr Speaker, Sir, AI will bring both disruption and opportunity.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: If managed well, it can raise productivity and expand opportunities for all.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: If we get this right, AI will not divide our workforce, it will strengthen it.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: And in doing so, we will renew this compact for AI-enabled growth.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: One where every Singaporean, whether working with code or with their hands, has a place and a role and a future in our economy.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: Around me, drivers and pedestrians looked up – a mix of curiosity and something quieter.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: A low, humming anxiety, fringed with a dash of awe.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: And behind their eyes, a very human question: what does this mean for me?

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: AI and autonomous technology are transforming the way we work, live and play, faster than any technology humankind has seen.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: So, the question this House must answer today is not how these technologies work, but what we are doing – concretely, deliberately – to make sure our workers' lives and livelihoods are not left behind.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: And I want to speak to it not with mere assurances, but with a plan.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: A plan for our workers, a plan for our union members, a plan for our brothers and sisters sitting up in the gallery supporting us in this Motion.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: The transformation is already happening, quietly, all around us.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: At Changi Airport, autonomous baggage tractors ferry luggage between terminals.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: At Marina Barrage Service Road, autonomous sweepers clear leaves and litter.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: But job redesign is equally critical to re-engineer existing jobs for new realities, to create new job types and to support workers through transitions as AI reshapes job longevity.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: And for job redesign to truly move the needle, it must be a genuine, ground-up effort with workers and their real workflows at the centre.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: First, consult workers deliberately, to really understand their work.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: As Executive Secretary of the National Transport Workers' Union (NTWU), I have seen first-hand what it looks like when tripartism works.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: Our management partners, SBS Transit, SMRT and others, have been preparing our bus captains and technicians for the advent of AI, electric vehicles (EVs) and AVs.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: Government supports companies and workers through that process.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: And unions, we do what we do best at: listening carefully on the ground to what workers truly need.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: It is exactly that ground listening that surfaced something we would have otherwise missed.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: Unlike conventional buses that use mirrors, EVs use digital monitors and our captains told us about the time delay, the glare, the eye strain and in more severe cases, nausea.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: They asked for longer training and preparatory times.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: The union pushed for it with our tripartite partners and it was addressed.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: But it directly shapes bus design, driver safety and passenger experience.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: That is a resource we must keep on tapping.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: These are sentiments shared by transport workers worldwide.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: Yet one in three of our Singaporeans, also remained confident that drivers would continue to play an important role.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: We sat with bus captains and asked them to walk us through a day's work, not what their job description said, but what they actually did.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: What they told us turned our assumptions upside down.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: On paper, we assumed driving was the core of a bus captain's job, perhaps, 80% of their tasks.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: The other 80%, helping elderly passengers board safely, managing crowding, de-escalating difficult situations, giving directions, being a calm and reassuring presence on board and even telling passengers they can only have a singing performance when seated – these are deeply human responsibilities that no AV can replace.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: If we had acted on our paper assumptions about the bus captain role, we would have misjudged job sizes, skill requirements and salary structures – creating inequitable outcomes for workers and human resource (HR) planning disasters for organisations alike.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: Getting the job description right is not a bureaucratic exercise.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: It is the foundation on which all of job redesign rests.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: But we cannot do this alone, not if we are serious about job redesign at scale.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: I call on the Government to resource this properly: to fund systematic study and mapping of actual job roles and workflows, so that job redesign is built on ground truths and not just assumptions.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: AI will transform work as we know it.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: But where exactly it will land – which tasks, which roles, which industries – nobody can fully predict that.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: That is precisely why the reimagination process matters so much.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: We have to build, prepare and yes, dare to dream of what an AI-powered workplace can look like together with our workers.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: The most important lesson I have taken from visiting companies in transformation is this: when you involve workers early and genuinely, they do not resist change.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: A Singapore SME, 25 years in business, in the business of data processing, which, at its heart, actually is what AI is.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: Rewind to 2001, Trusted Hub was handling Government submissions from members of the public; stacks and stacks of paper; photocopiers, faxes, prints.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: Fast forward to 2026, same business, more or less the same clients, but a completely different way of working.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: AI now processes much of the data, taking the load off their staff.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: What impressed me when I visited was not the technology.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: Because Trusted Hub brought their workers into the reimagination process as stakeholders – not passengers – the majority of their staff have upskilled themselves to programme AI Agents, creating both enterprise and innovation value for the company.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: And the oldest AI Agent programmer in the company?

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: And this is what happens when you do not underestimate your workers.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: I have spoken in this House before about FairPrice's Store of Tomorrow at Punggol Coast Mall, featured at international trade shows as a model for the supermarket of the future and a living showcase of how technology can make work better, easier and safer for our workers.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: It displaces fear not with words but with evidence people can walk into and see for themselves.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: But what made it work was not the AI.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: Workers and unions shaped and designed the system, not inherited it.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: And because of that, staff did not just accept the change, they owned it.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: And what I want is more of this.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: Stores of tomorrow, bus interchanges of tomorrow, restaurants of tomorrow, clinics of tomorrow.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: Living testbeds that allow reimagination to happen, not just within companies but across clusters and our communities, so that conversations about AI in the workplace can take place openly, candidly and with imagination, rather than dread.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: Very much like my Punggol residents watching our autonomous shuttles glide by, a low hum of anxiety, yes, but definitely fringed with a dash of awe.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: While the shape of tomorrow's workplace is still forming, one thing is clear.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: And it is a British entrepreneur who has started calling his AI bots, AI employees, to remind himself and his team that AI is not about replacing people but about changing roles.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: They are small, deliberate, but very significant acts that normalise AI in the workplace and make it something workers can see themselves thriving in rather than being displaced by.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: This involves responsible employers, progressive employees and indeed, a supportive and nurturing Government.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: It is the tripartite way and it is why the Tripartite Jobs Council matters so much to organise, to set the tone right from the start, on how AI is embedded and rewarded in everyday company life.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: Evidence that when workers are treated as co-creators, transformation is faster, adoption is stronger and outcomes are better for everyone.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: The Tripartite Jobs Council is well-placed to drive this reimagination work at every level, through Company Training Committees (CTCs), CTC Queen Bees at cluster level, sectoral AI uplift plans across industries.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: Our Queen Bees can bring their contractor ecosystems along, as what FairPrice did with their Store of Tomorrow.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: Unions will do what we do best: walk with workers and management through what the road ahead looks like, and what new roles are emerging along the way.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: Workers deserve to know not just that AI is coming, but where the next testbeds will be, what the new jobs will look like and how to get there.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: For workers standing at that crossroads, it is everything.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: And we should not paper over it with optimism.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: Hence, transition support must be real, it must be timely and it must reach those who need it most.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: We owe our workers a system that catches them before they fall too far and gets them back to a good job as quickly as possible.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: Not as an afterthought but as the first line of defence.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: If we redesign jobs well and early, we reduce the number of workers who need to be caught in the first place.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: The best transition support is one that makes the cliff shorter to begin with.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: That is why the signal we send to enterprises matters so much.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: This will be the assurance to workers that Singapore's AI transition will not result in jobless growth and that we keep the transition time to a new good job as short as possible.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: As Advisor to the National Taxi Association and the National Private Hire Vehicles Association, I want to speak directly to that.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: (In Mandarin):   Our taxi and private-hire drivers are already navigating a fiercely competitive environment with high fuel costs.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: Seeing AVs operating in Punggol and hearing news of autonomous bus pilots, they cannot help but harbour a quiet, unspoken worry.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: They are not asking us to halt technological progress – but what they need is not just reassurance.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: How will the geofencing of autonomous vehicles be progressively expanded?

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: New roles such as remote operators and safety supervisors are beginning to emerge.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: I hope that drivers who are willing will be supported and given access to training, so that they can transition into these new positions.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: This is not just a matter that concerns platform drivers.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: Our technicians and tradesmen keep Singapore running with their hands, yet in conversations about AI, they are often invisible.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: We must press on to build career pathways for tradesmen that are more promising and more respected, while harnessing AI to enhance their capabilities – not to replace their judgement. : Mr Speaker, the workers most exposed to AI disruption are often the ones with the least buffer – least savings, least flexibility, least time to wait for a system to catch up with them.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: That is why our response must be tripartite in the fullest sense.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: Unions will do what we have always done, walk the ground, listen and shape livelihood opportunities alongside our workers and we will continue to "jaga rumah" – by keeping watch on what other jurisdictions are doing, from China's Internet court ruling that AI replacement alone is not grounds for dismissals to California's requirement for human safety operators on AVs.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: These are signals of a world working out where the boundaries are.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: Singapore must learn from them, and when necessary, get ahead of them.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: Government must design transition support around the people who need it and not around what is administratively convenient.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: This is a standard we must hold ourselves to.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: It requires sitting with workers, understanding what their work really is, not just what the job description says, and going back to the ground when the first answer turns out to be incomplete, as ours was with bus captains.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: Companies need to be supported through this and not just pushed into it.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: And I look to our leading companies, our Queen Bees, to step forward, share what has been worked on, and bring their sectors along with them.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: Transformation that stays within one company is transformation that is only half done.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: Our unions, our e2i, our Tripartite Jobs Council – we are already on the ground, in the companies, with our CTCs, sitting across the table from workers and employers every day.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: We have trust that took many, many years to build.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: The SWDA and our agencies must build on this.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: Our workers watching it are not asking us to stop it.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: They are asking us to make sure that as it moves forward, they move forward too.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: I believe that an AI transition with no jobless growth is possible.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: Not because the technology will take care of it, but because we will.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: If we consult workers properly, involve them in the reimagination of their work and back that up with transition support that actually reaches the people who need it most.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: I declare my interest as the owner and director of a company that provides software to training providers.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: For decades, Singapore's economic model has been built on the premise that a highly educated and skilled workforce would hold the keys to a prosperous future and be a buffer against economic storms.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: However, we are now in the midst of a paradigm shift where AI is not only augmenting human capability, but in many ways replacing it.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Unlike past economic cycles, where such turbulence could be written off as an episode of creative destruction, AI promises to be a harbinger of a fundamental shift in our economic and social relationships.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Taking this concept further, it would even impact the roles that the Government plays in mediating between the individual and society.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Today, we must recognise that the very nature of labour's economic power is changing.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Failure to address this issue, even as productivity soars, will lead to an entrenched lower and middle class with the loss of economic agency.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This concern is articulated by Jasmine Sun in an opinion piece for the New York Times, where she identifies the San Francisco consensus, a growing recognition that the hiring of young workers in highly AI exposed occupations is already in decline.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: She reminds us of the risk of a resulting permanent underclass, where the gains of technology are concentrated in the hands of a very few.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: However, overall employment effects have so far been modest as productivity gains offsets some displacement.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: It should be noted that these studies examined early and controlled deployments.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: As agentic AI scales across entire industries simultaneously, the distributional consequences may be more severe and swifter than early productivity research would suggest.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: We cannot be certain which trajectory Singapore is on.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The asymmetry of risk demands that we prepare for the harder scenario, not the easier one.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This concern is shared by the very architects of the AI revolution.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: He argued that the proactive redistribution of AI-driven wealth, including giving citizens equity stakes in the economy, could make this a broadly prosperous transition.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Similarly, Dario Amodei, the CEO of Anthropic, has observed that the health of a democracy is premised on the average person having leveraged through creating economic value, a view he expressed in his 2024 essay, "Machines of Loving Grace".

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The erosion of that leverage is a deeply concerning prospect that requires a bold and structural policy response.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Singapore is uniquely positioned to lead this response and to capture the genuine economic opportunities AI presents for our people.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: As a small, open economy with a highly educated workforce, strong institutions and well-capitalised sovereign wealth funds, we have the tools to act swiftly and structurally, compared to many large nations.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: But that window of opportunity will not remain open indefinitely.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: While cost arbitrage makes offshoring attractive, AI could erode that advantage – not by bringing those jobs back but by enabling small teams of skilled Singaporeans to do the work that once required hundreds of offshore workers.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The opportunity is not in reshoring in a traditional sense but the concentration of higher-value orchestration and oversight roles here at home, where trust, institutional quality and proximity to decision-makers matter.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: A blue-collar worker who struggles with English could dictate in their mother tongue and have AI render as professional documentation in real time, freeing them to focus on their craft rather than their grammar.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: AI should be an equaliser that elevates the technical master, not a wedge that stratifies our workforce.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: AI tools can also power a new breed of local startups by enabling small hyper-efficient teams to create immense value and scale, achieving global reach with minimal manpower.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Singapore must therefore be at the forefront of this shift while ensuring that benefits accrue to all citizens.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This will require workers and entrepreneurs who are trained, skilled and adept at harnessing AI tools and innovations and empowering their employees to do the same.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: These programmes enrich training providers while leaving workers with skills that have little economic value.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This misalignment risks creating a two-speed economy where capital owners and tech-integrated firms leave behind those stuck in the slow lane of traditional employment, leading to a fundamental erosion of social cohesion and increasing the risk of long-term structural unemployment.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This fund is a necessary safeguard to maintain the integrity of our social contract.
