speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: It is a strategic surplus transfer from enterprises which benefit immensely from AI back to Singaporeans to facilitate our collective stability.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: I will elaborate on the precise funding mechanisms shortly after I explain the uses of the fund.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: I propose the fund be organised in two distinct pillars.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: It is not meant to replace income, but to provide a tangible signal that every Singaporean has ownership in our shared future.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This would serve as a social floor, ensuring that the gains from national digital prosperity provide tangible peace of mind and dignity for all.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This dividend will provide an additional cushion for families as the nature of work evolves.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: It also allows Singapore to reap the full productivity benefits of AI without overly exacerbating social inequality.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: An argument could be made that the Community Development Council (CDC) vouchers already do this, but those are entirely discretionary.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The social dividend I propose is a structural entitlement – a function of receipts rather than what the fiscal mood of the moment happens to be.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: That distinction matters enormously for a family planning its future.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This rewards the worker's effort in adapting while lowering the barrier for firms to hire, train and retain talent in this volatile market.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Recognising that many SMEs lack the capacity to design structured OJT programmes, I propose that the fund also finance a pool of expert OJT consultants.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: These consultants experienced in OJT design will rotate between firms to structure OJT blueprints tailored to each firm's specific needs.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This will help SMEs fill their talent gap while also addressing the need to create new steps in the ladder of training and apprenticeships for new entrants into the marketplace.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Furthermore, I suggest a mentorship credit be provided to employers to compensate senior staff for the time they spend on structured mentorship, turning our workplaces into true academies of mastery and ensuring that skills remain relevant to the actual needs of the economy.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The mastery fund should be made available to all business entities and societies that are founded and based in Singapore, including micro enterprises.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The use of funds should be closely monitored to ensure that it genuinely contributes to AI mastery within each firm.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: I estimate the annual cost of the mastery fund to be approximately $1.42 billion.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: By focusing on these companies, we capture the automation surplus from those best positioned to drive growth through AI rather than headcount.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Whether global tech firms or traditional giants, these enterprises are at the forefront of decoupling revenue from labour.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This tax increase will generate an estimated $1.5 billion annually, ensuring that gains from record-breaking efficiency are recycled back into the National AI Equity Fund for the benefit of all Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Based on current estimates, this would raise approximately $1.45 billion annually.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Our sovereign wealth entities, GIC and Temasek, have been early movers into the AI space, investing in foundational firms like Anthropic and committing billions to the AI infrastructure partnership alongside Microsoft, BlackRock and Nvidia.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: As these global Investments profit from the automation of labour worldwide, it is only right that we recycle a modest portion of those gains back into our own workforce.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: It ensures our reserves provide more than just financial stability, but also the long-term economic agency of every Singaporean.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: As we look toward the future, we cannot simply assume that displaced workers will transition smoothly into new roles as they have in previous technological revolutions.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The steam engine did not replace human judgement, but AI may do just that.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: That is precisely why passive reskilling is insufficient and why the financial security of a social dividend is needed.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Workers shifting towards less automatable roles in entrepreneurship, care work, the skilled trades, sports and the arts do not just need training, but time and security to make that leap.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Certainly, new jobs will emerge that we cannot yet imagine, but we must build a system robust enough to support our people even if that emergence is slower or more unevenly distributed than we would otherwise hope.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The National AI Equity Fund provides a financial buffer for Singaporeans to make these transitions with confidence.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: We cannot allow AI to become a wedge that fractures our society.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Instead, we must use it to become the greatest equaliser our nation has ever known.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Let us make it our goal to ensure that as machines grow more capable, our people grow more secure.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: By acting now, we can ensure that technological progress serves the dignity and economic agency of every Singaporean.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: Much has also been said by the Government about how the global disruption will impact our play, our work and our lives.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: In policy-making, there is always the binary choice: ride this AI wave or be submerged and be left behind.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: This is Hobson’s choice and the answer is obvious.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: But we cannot ask a question of a strawman.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: Singapore is a small, open and digitally connected economy.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: AI will be a fact of economic life.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: The Government has said that it will grow our economy, support our businesses and take care of our workers.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: But there is a difference between policy-making in the Ministries and implementation on the ground.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: At street level, the AI transition looks intimidating, expensive, and for many middle-aged workers, a place of anxiety and confusion.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: This is the first wave of change and may be the hardest.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: The Government, businesses, unions and workers must struggle together to ride out this wave.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: During the transition, some jobs will disappear, but new jobs will also emerge.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: Left to the market, there will only be growth where the strongest, fittest and most able benefit.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: In a city where the law of the economic jungle operates unfettered, let us be honest, the AI transition will benefit some, but not all.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: This growth will not lead to better and more prosperous lives for all.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: But that is not the job for the market.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: That is our job; all of us here in this House must bend the market to our will: to create more high-value jobs for Singaporeans and retrain displaced workers but to do so in a way that also meets the business imperative for profits, so that our economy can continue to grow in the long run.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: We have built Singapore on solutions that met both interests in the past, and we must do so again in the future.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: If businesses close down, more workers will lose their jobs, even those not threatened by AI.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: Our businesses have faced worsening labour shortages over the past decade.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: In particular, many jobs that Singaporeans cannot or will not do are done by non-Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: For instance, heavy duty roles in construction, maritime and aviation sectors, that are exposed to the harsh elements of a warming climate.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: This will be a game changer for us.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: The next frontier is in physical generative AI or embodied AI.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: In more recent times, generative AI technologies have been integrated with physical systems, enabling machines to interact with and adapt to the real world.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: It enables robots to learn complex tasks, such as manipulation and navigation, via simulation and transferring intelligence from digital models to real world hardware.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: Put simply, robots and humanoids capable of thinking and even perceiving, can be deployed in unstructured and dynamic environments, to assist or even replace human workers.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: In recent months, companies such as Dexterity AI, Figure AI and Unitree Robotics have demonstrated their capabilities in AI-powered robots and humanoids in specialised roles.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: Unlike generative AI tools like ChatGPT that trawl the Internet to train its models, physical generative AI tools need to be trained in contextualised environments for the roles and tasks they are set out to do.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: Over time, these physical AI capabilities will mature and become accessible to businesses facing manpower shortage.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: These AI-powered robots can help our businesses overcome manpower constraints, lower costs and increase profitability.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: Physical AI robots are good at repetitive tasks but cannot replace every single role.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: Jobs and process redesigned into man-machine hybrid teams will be the new norm.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: Seniors and women can join the transformed workforce – with repetitive, heavy-duty roles done by robots and complex supervisory roles performed by humans.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: It will be a new model of freedom and empowerment, unimaginable today but a reality in the very near future.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: Singaporeans can be upskilled as supervisors of robots.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: New high-value job roles such as design, build and maintenance of these AI robots will be created for young engineers and technicians.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: More Singaporeans can retire at a later age if they wish to, since their roles will become less physically demanding.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: Seniors and women can join industries previously dominated by those with stronger physical abilities.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: Prime Minister Lawrence Wong outlined four key pillars for our National AI Strategy.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: In particular, in the Advanced Manufacturing and Transport Connectivity sectors, AI-powered robots will indeed be the force-multiplier.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: We are well-positioned for it, but we must move fast.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: And I would suggest the following six steps.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: Three, workers should also step up, learn new skills and be open to new job opportunities.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: All IHL students should learn AI tools relevant for their disciplines.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: Six, businesses should be open to work with AI companies to automate and redesign work processes, revamp job roles and create man and machine hybrid teams.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: Physical AI can ease labour shortages and reshape work into human machine teams.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: With job redesign, upskilling and education reform, workers can move into higher value roles, while businesses can grow with higher productivity.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: Technology companies create AI solutions, businesses own them and workers leverage them.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: AI must be used as a force for good and not for criminal and harmful exploits.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: Establishing the ethics around AI use will make the difference between our society benefiting from the use of AI or becoming enslaved by it.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: But there is also a deeper moral question relating to AI.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: AI is artificial; it has no intrinsic good, no value in and of itself.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: We, in this House, have a duty to bend the market in the use of AI, not just to forbid what is criminal but to enable what is fair, good and just.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: We must ensure that the AI transition does not merely create growth but creates jobs, benefits workers, strengthens businesses and elevates communities.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: (In Mandarin):   Mr Speaker, Singapore's AI shift needs a coordinated effort by Government, businesses, unions and workers to ensure that both businesses and employees stand to benefit, and to support and assist those who are affected.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: This includes providing retraining and expanding the scope of education, creating higher-value jobs so that more Singaporeans can adapt to these changes as quickly as possible.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: Physical AI – robots combined with generative AI – can ease labour shortages by taking on tough and risky work in sectors, such as construction, aviation and maritime, while reshaping roles into human-machine teams.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: A national transformation should not merely be pursued for the sake of higher economic growth, but should ensure that all segments of society can benefit. : Mr Speaker, the Motion on which I rise to speak today asks for us to affirm that AI transition "must not lead to jobless growth".

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: And this "must" is not an empirical prediction, nor is it empty rhetoric.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: AI in this free market may or may not be the new model of freedom and empowerment for our people.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: It is our resolve that makes it so.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Prime Minister, the Labour Chief, the Government as a whole, have all said the same in the past months; that this is what they intend.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: What I want to examine this afternoon is whether the policy architecture we have is equal to the commitment we are being asked to affirm.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The firm can use AI to make its existing workers more capable, more productive, more valuable than they were before or it can use AI to do without those workers entirely.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The economist's shorthand for this is augmentation as opposed to automation: augmentation where AI works alongside the worker, and automation where AI replaces them.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Stanford economist, Eric Brynjolfsson, one of the leading academic voices on AI and labour markets, has made a convincing case that in an unaided market without deliberate policies steering in the other direction, incentives systematically favour automation.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Firms find it easier and cheaper to deploy AI to replace workers than to retrain them.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The tax code, the labour market institutions, the cost structures of capital all tilt the playing field.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Even though augmentation creates more total value over time, more good jobs, broader prosperity and a fairer distribution of the gains, the default trajectory of an unguided system is automation.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Government's chosen and declared direction is augmentation.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Labour Chief in this Chamber yesterday put the same commitment in his own words – not AI instead of workers but AI working for workers.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The philosophical direction is settled across the aisle.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The substantive question is whether our policy architecture matches it.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: There are three places where architecture is currently miscalibrated.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Three places where, today, the system is permitting automation despite promises to the contrary.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Labour Chief yesterday said that AI is also reshaping professional, manager and executive (PME) jobs in higher-end professions, like doctors, lawyers and accountants.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Prime Minister has said much the same – AI will affect Singapore's professionals, managers and technicians (PMETs) who have spent years building specialist careers and who are now being told that the ground below them is moving.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: At his May Day rally last week, Prime Minister Lawrence Wong said, "We may not be able to protect every job, but we will protect every worker." The question is whether the instrument the Government has chosen, the SkillsFuture Job Seeker Support scheme, delivers on that promise.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Prime Minister has termed the Job Seeker Support scheme the "Singapore way", a more pragmatic, more Singaporean alternative to the redundancy insurance that is the Workers' Party's (WP's) preferred solution.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: By that test, the tradition has long been built on investments of exactly that kind.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Central Provident Fund (CPF), MediShield Life, MediSave, these are all universal contributary schemes paid out when life's major contingencies hit.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Each catches every worker because the contingency it insures against can hit every worker.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Jobseeker Support scheme is not built in that tradition.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is a tax-funded grant gated on pre-redundancy income, closer in design to a means-tested assistance than to insurance against contingency.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If this proposal is adopted, it is movement in the direction that the WP has long argued for.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But Mr Ng's proposal moves the line, ours would remove it.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Raising the ceiling lets more workers into the scheme but it does not change what the scheme does for them.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For those who do qualify under the ceiling, the taper carries its own message: a payment that starts high and slowly reduces is not a flaw.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And a countdown pushes a worker to take the first offer, not the right one.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: MOM's own data tells us why this matters.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: So, they took what was available and not what their experience was worth.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Most of us have experienced how the higher up the career ladder you climb, the longer it takes for you to find your next role.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is funded by employer-employee contributions in the same model as the CPF and it covers every worker who pays in, including the professionals the Labour Chief has identified as the most exposed because the contingency it insures against does not stop at $5,000, $7,600 or any other ceiling Parliament may set.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Prime Minister said we must protect every worker.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The instrument the Government has selected does not.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But what does our tax code say to the firm at that decision point?

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: These are good things to reward, but what the architecture does not currently do is reward the choice itself.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: A firm that retrenches its existing workers and trains a smaller set of new hires receive the same fiscal treatment as a firm that retain and retrains its existing workforce.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: A firm that buys AI to replace workers receives the same fiscal treatment as a firm that buys AI to augment them.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The tax code is silent at the fork.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And as Bronson previously observed, silence at the fork is not neutrality in consequence.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: When the tax code does not actively reward retention, the underlying economics tilts firms toward retrenchment.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Labour is, after all, the most expensive line on the balance sheet and labour costs are permanent in a way that one-off training costs are not.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Yesterday, Mr Ng defended the CTC framework in this Chamber as the mechanism that ties enterprise transformation to worker progression and proposed expanding it through the new Tripartite Jobs Council.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: CTC operates at the project level for firms that engage with it, with grant funding attached, expanding its reach scales the grant model, but does not change the broader fiscal architecture that every firm operates within, whether or not it is within the CTC scheme.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And it is this broader fiscal architecture that shapes chief financial officers' financial decision-making at the decision point.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is this missing conditional piece that will give firms a fiscal signal precisely at the point where they have to make a decision.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This retraining tax credit would reward a proactive choice instead of simply investing in AI.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The fourth limb of this Motion affirms that economic progress must remain inclusive.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: That is a commitment about distribution, not just growth.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The instrument I am proposing today is the diagnostic tool that any redistributive mechanism, including Mr Giam's, needs to operate on.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Because the third condition for an augmentation strategy, to be real, is verification.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It makes a prediction that wages in the sectors where AI is being deployed alongside workers, will track the productivity gains that these workers helped to create.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If that prediction holds, the framework that the Government has adopted is being delivered as advertised.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If productivity rises in these sectors, but wages do not move alongside it, then what is being delivered is something other than augmentation, whatever language we use to describe it.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Right now, we have very few mechanisms and very few systematic ways of telling which is occurring.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Public funds are flowing into these sectors and more through the CTC grants, the newly formed Tripartite Jobs Council, the Skills and Workforce Development Agency and various enterprise transformation programmes.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Over time, its scope and coverage can be expanded.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In February, in my Budget speech, I framed this as a distribution question.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Today, with this Motion before the House asking us to affirm that economic progress must remain inclusive, I propose it again as something more fundamental.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The AI gains audit is the most direct instrument available to Parliament to test whether the Government's chosen direction of augmentation is actually being delivered.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If the gains are being shared with workers, the audit will say so and the framework will have evidence to back its claim.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If they are not, we will know before the gap becomes a chasm and before this Motion becomes a statement of hope rather than of policy.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is made every day by the architecture of the schemes we run, the tax code we maintain and the data we choose to collect.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Whatever the House says today, that architecture will keep making the choice on our behalf.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Right now, my position is that the architecture pushes workers towards the first available job rather than the right one.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And that is why I support this Motion.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I urge the Government to give it the architecture it requires so that we can make sure that no worker is left behind.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: I rise in support of the Motion, an AI Transition with No Jobless Growth.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: It is not a pilot; it is already becoming a platform.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: The broader question is whether we grow without leaving our workers behind.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: In the next decade, Singapore should be judged not by how fast we deploy AI, by how well we translate adoption into better jobs, better wages and stronger trust at the workplace.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: I speak in three roles today as a professional, as a parent and as a Member of Parliament listening to my residents.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Many PMETs, they are not afraid of technology, they are uneasy about the uncertainty because AI rarely replaces the whole job.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: It unbundles tasks, it compresses teams, it changes what employers hire for.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: And when you cannot see how your role evolves, anxiety rises.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Parents today ask very simple questions: will my child have a fair start?

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: And if entry-level work shrinks, who will then train the next generation?

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Third, the resident anxiety and this is the most practical one.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Many people cannot just stop their work to train or retrain.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: They are asking simply for a fair chance and a system that they can navigate.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: AI is smart, but it is not wise.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: It can hallucinate, it can sound confident and yet still be wrong.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: So, the future should not be about humans competing with AI.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: It should be about humans working with AI, with judgement, with verification and with accountability.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: It is about trust, job redesign and the worker journey in whole.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Trust will determine if this adoption would succeed.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: If AI is experienced by workers as surveillance, the trust will thin and eventually break.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: And when trust breaks, adoption will slow and gains will not be sustainable.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: This is the direction we should double down on and I offer four practical moves on this front.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: First, skills must be a pathway and not a menu.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: But on the ground, many workers tell me this.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: It is useful, but it is also overwhelming.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Too many courses, too many badges, too little signal.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: So, the problem now is not just access.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: This could mean higher subsidy tiers or outcome-linked support, such as completion plus interview, attachment or redeployment pathways subject to design and feasibility.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: If we fund adoption, we should ask, how will tasks change, how will workers be redeployed and how will the performance measurements continue to remain fair?

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Productivity must show up as better work and, ultimately, better wages for our workers and not only a shrinking headcount.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: This is where our tripartite partners can help with playbooks, with templates and advisory support so that SMEs are not left alone to figure it out.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Third, bring AI readiness to the professional sectors, like clinics, law firms, accounting firms.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: They want to adopt AI but they worry about safety, confidentiality, liability and trust.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: One practical model already shared in this House is already emerging in healthcare.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: For our workers, support should begin when need is recognised.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: That means faster job matching, modular training that fits real-life schedules and practical guidance for responsible transitions.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: In practice, structured coaching and a clear next step reduces anxiety, because it shifts a worker from waiting to acting.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: They worry that jobs may disappear, that the value of skills may diminish and what may happen to the future of children.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: The questions are also difficult, but our response is not to fear.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: AI is advancing quickly, but human mercy, trust, sense of justice, creativity, language, culture – all these cannot be fully replaced by any machine.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: AI can compute; but the human connection, human judgement and the human responsibility will always remain with us.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: So, we must move ourselves from the path of fear to the path of opportunity.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: The rise of AI does not mean that humans are no longer needed.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Rather, it makes it clearer on what truly are the important tasks that humans must do.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: In this regard, the humanities are important; language skills are important; cultural nuances are important; social understanding is important.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Healthcare, caregiving, education, social services, counselling and work that involves direct contact with people – these are fields that AI cannot replace.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: The Tamil language and Tamil culture are a support in this endeavour; our literature nurtures the human feeling.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: So, this is what we must tell our young people: embrace AI but also grow the human capability.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: It is a path, a belief, a plan for the future.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Let us have faith. : Mr Speaker, Sir, no jobless growth must mean one thing.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: The test is not how many schemes we have.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Whether a parent can feel confident about their child's runway and future, and whether the citizen's journey feels seamless.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: With these observations, Mr Speaker, I support the Motion.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Our technological infrastructure and initiatives to upskill our workers are key parts of how we plan to confront the disruptions and opportunities presented to us by this new and rapidly developing technology.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: However, we must also recognise and act on an additional uncomfortable reality.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: International estimates suggest that around 60% of workers in advanced economies are in jobs that are highly exposed to AI.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: How is AI fundamentally reconfiguring our labour market?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This can be understood through three distinct shifts.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: First, many existing jobs will be transformed from within.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: AI is taking, or has already taken, over routine information processing tasks – drafting, summarising, extracting data and standardising analysis.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Managers, health professionals and legal professionals are already using AI tools to handle these types of tasks, freeing up time for judgement, complex problem-solving and human interaction.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: In what economists call high exposure, low complementarity roles, AI can perform most of the core tasks on its own and there are fewer reasons to keep humans in the loop.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Advances in agentic AI technology and models have only sharpened this impact.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: In the UK, some financial institutions, like investment banks, have relooked their hiring of fresh graduates for certain roles because of AI's automation capabilities.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Third, AI will also create new jobs and new demands.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: We are already seeing rising demand for AI engineers, data scientists and AI-product specialists, but also for data-savvy professionals across finance, healthcare, logistics and education.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: These new roles tend to offer higher wages, but only for workers who can supply the right mix of technical and complementary human skills.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Yes, indeed, the AI job transformation is already here and we are in the midst of a major disruption.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Yet, the impact will not be uniform across all professions, nor is it, and will it, affect our society and economy evenly.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: For now, AI disruption is strongest amongst white-collared workers, especially entry-level roles.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Unlike previous technological disruptions that have historically affected blue-collared jobs, AI today will most affect cognitive, white-collared roles – a call centre agent, an admin officer or a junior business support executive, whose workday is built around standard processes, routine reports and scripted responses, is in a role where AI can perform almost all core tasks.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: In such high exposure, low complementarity white-collar roles, employers can consolidate positions, slow hiring or redesign jobs to ensure that fewer people are expected to do more with AI as a simple justification.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: If we do not address this, the benefits of AI will end up with only a small group of workers.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Research suggests that productivity and wealth gains could disproportionately accrue to those best positioned to leverage AI capabilities.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: One documented economic effect of high-skill job creation is increased local service demand.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Even if such spillover effects generate more jobs, the quality and availability of these jobs for vulnerable workers is less certain to me.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: In Singapore, lower wage and routine-intensive roles are more likely to be held by vulnerable worker groups who may also face greater displacement risk from automation.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The extent to which spillover effects from AI-driven growth would benefit lower-income workers remains uncertain.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: We need Singapore-specific research, modelling these distributional impacts and to make this data publicly available, to inform more targeted policy responses.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: We must also remember that Singaporeans are already feeling the strain of rising property prices and higher cost for essential services.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: They have been building for some time as we are a small, open economy, significantly dependent on capital inflows.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Would AI's effects drive further unequal wealth accumulation?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: It is, therefore, a fair and pressing question to ask: could AI-driven economic activity inadvertently add to daily cost pressures?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Beyond broad economic pressures, we must turn toward the human face of this transition.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: As jobs continue to be reshaped and workers continue to be upskilled, we cannot leave behind those who face systemic barriers as our nation progresses towards an AI-ready future.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Amongst them are persons with disabilities, women, lower-income Singaporeans, as well as young graduates.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: AI can introduce new forms of discrimination against persons with disabilities.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: As AI algorithms are often trained via pattern recognition, they arrive at determinations based on common patterns within datasets.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Thus, if skilled historical data is being used to train AI for, for example, recruitment processes, AI might reinforce this bias for job applications from persons with disabilities and any other group which historically, is not well represented in this space.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Female workers, too, face a heightened risk of marginalisation from AI.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Altogether, this means that they are less represented in what is regarded as the safe side of AI.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: They would thus be less well positioned to benefit where AI compliments high-skill work.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Female workers are less likely to gain from AI's benefits, while remaining more vulnerable to displacement.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: In short, women face higher risk and have fewer opportunities.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: For our young graduates, new uncertainty has been introduced by the way AI has been reshaping jobs.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The erosion of entry-level jobs has presented a catch-22 dilemma for Generation Zs.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: While companies are still looking to hire professionals for experienced roles, young graduates have fewer opportunities to gain such experiences as jobs are absorbed by AI.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Adding to this is recent research, which has shown that simply being aware of AI's potential to augment or threaten one's job can increase burn-out, mainly by heightening job insecurity and emotional exhaustion amongst workers.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: While AI is often associated with disruption to white-collar work, vulnerable workers and families face significant risks too.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Unequal access to AI tools and training could entrench existing disadvantages.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Those without the resources of home or home environments conducive to learning new skills may find themselves falling further behind.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: If left unaddressed, then this risks hardening inequality across generations.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Measuring impact on Singapore beyond economic output, what does this all mean for Singapore?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Just this past week, we have seen the launch of the Marriage and Parenthood Reset Work Group.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: What is the effect of AI advances on our birth rate?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Economic insecurity has already been cited by young Singaporeans as a reason for delaying or foregoing parenthood, but the barriers go beyond finances.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Job uncertainty erodes a sense of stability and confidence in the future, the feeling that one has a firm enough footing to build a family and put down roots.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: If AI-driven disruption deepens this broader sense of insecurity, we can reasonably expect further downward pressure on our already tragically low total fertility rate.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The Government has to be even more targeted in ensuring that all workers, regardless of their gender, age, occupation, income and accessibility needs, are fully prepared for the disruption caused by AI, to ease financial pressures on vulnerable workers who are made redundant.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This will minimise the uncertainty and toll of unemployment on both workers and their families as AI displacement becomes more commonplace.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: To ensure our policies are working, we need more public data for us to measure AI-driven disruptions on our labour market.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: For example, how we measure the success of our AI programmes.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: It is a good start, but they do not tell us the effects of AI programmes and disruptions on different groups of society.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: These measures focus on throughput rather than equity.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: We need data on wage trajectories, job quality and retention in AI roles two to three years after the programme is completed.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: First, the participant data profile should have more details made public.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This can include previous occupations, income band before training, age, gender, education and disability status.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This allows us to see where participants come from.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: High exposure, low complementarity roles, or already high complementarity roles.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This will inform if vulnerable groups are even putting their feet through the door.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Next, more accurately measuring AI disruption in the wider labour market can come in the form of exposure complementarity mapping, thus understanding whether jobs are high exposure and low complementarity, and to establish a tuned framework to track displacement, wage changes and job quality across demographic groups.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Such data gives the Government a clearer picture of how AI is affecting different communities, so that support can be directed where it is most needed.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: I will now turn to some thoughts on how our youths can address the challenges of AI.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: If AI displaces a significant share of entry level roles, young workers may find fewer opportunities to build the foundational experience traditionally needed to progress into senior positions.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: One of our nation's solutions could be to better encourage and support entrepreneurship amongst youths.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This will allow them to also gain valuable skills independently, rather than wait to be picked up to be employed by an established firm.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This approach builds on an already open door.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: We need a culture and framework that recognise the value of a failed startup, or that support founder-led networks over time.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Drawing on lessons from other entrepreneurial hubs, what are the areas that have inhibited Singapore's ability to establish a more sustainable ecosystem conducive for entrepreneurs?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: First, we must continue to build sustained informal networks that made an entrepreneurship culture self-sustaining.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Our current networks are often programme based and time limited, skewed towards short-term coaching.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Yet research shows that informal mentorships arising from mutual choice and affinity are far more effective than administrative matching.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: If mentorship is only linked to short-term grants, our youths may miss out on the benefits that accrue from the trust-based guidance that can be seen in, for example, Silicon Valley.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: In leading entrepreneurial hubs like Silicon Valley and Shenzhen, informal founder networks have been a critical but often overlooked driver of success.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: They enable knowledge sharing, supply chain connections and a spin-off of new ventures from anchor firms.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: How can we reduce administrative burden on founders to ensure that they do not become overly occupied with meeting grant milestones instead of establishing the market competitiveness they need to survive AI-driven disruption.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: One possibility is to limit formal reporting to end of grant rather than more regularly to strike a balance.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Singapore must also better leverage our anchor firms.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Companies like Grab, Sea and Singtel hold deep reservoirs of technical expertise and industry networks that largely remain locked within the firm.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Could we use targeted tax credits or co-investment matching for peer development programmes to encourage anchor firms to run structured mentorship and spin-out programmes for early-stage founders?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This will allow organic networks to form around existing reservoirs of excellence, rather than hope that Government grant cycles will do so.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The private sector must lead, and the Government's role should shift from convener and gatekeeper to catalyst.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This is how we can start to grow our entrepreneurial system from within industry.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Singapore's culture of economic emphasis and social conformity makes us sometimes afraid to fail.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Founders have to make decisions with incomplete information and meaningful innovation has to be backed up by some freedom to fail.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: We have to treat failure as a stepping stone rather than a stigma, or we end up stifling the very ecosystem we are trying to build and leave our youths ill-equipped to flourish in an age of disruption.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: We can do so by beginning our own transition towards a better space for entrepreneurship, encourage experimentation and normalise entrepreneurial failure as growth and experience.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Failure should be a stepping stone, not a dead end.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: And we began this transition within schools where we have to move away from perfect scores, where we have entrepreneurial projects in schools which expose students to the inner workings of a startup.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: We should also showcase failed projects for their bonus.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Singapore's current bankruptcy framework can also be re-examined to better support entrepreneurs.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Could we explore a dedicated pathway for bona fide startup failure, one that allows founders to be discharged sooner, resume directorship more quickly and have their experience recognised as something valuable rather than a liability.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: It is not to make failure consequence free, but to ensure that the cost of an honest bet gone wrong does not permanently deter our most enterprising young Singaporeans from trying again.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Singapore comes from a place of strength and we are already intentionally deciding to lead the way when it comes to setting the agenda in global AI governance.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Our stewardship role must extend beyond frameworks, and we have to play our part in addressing global imbalances in AI development and use reflected in recent data.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: There is justifiable concern about how vulnerable groups and the global South are woefully underrepresented in the AI space.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: As responsible world citizens, we can do our part to address this.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This is not merely an abstract foreign policy and ambition.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: It has direct consequences for jobs here at home.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: In recent weeks, a plane has been circling San Francisco with a banner that reads, "Stop Hiring Humans." The same message appears on billboards and bus shelters across the city, alongside slogans such as "The Era of AI Employees Is Here." The campaign is the work of Artisan, an AI startup.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It reflects a fear that the future of work may exclude people rather than empower them.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: I rise in support of this Motion because that must not be Singapore’s approach.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: AI must not be a signal to workers that they are dispensable.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: In my work in Temasek, I have seen how technology disrupts industries, and I want to lay out my key thesis upfront.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: In the Temasek ecosystem, many companies are already investing in AI.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Tools are being deployed and pilots are multiplying.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: But the real constraint we are seeing is not technology, compute, or capital.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We are working closely with Chief Human Resource Officers and Chief Technology Officers to bridge the gap between adoption and actual value creation.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Where skill supply lags, opportunity does not disappear.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The AI transition we are debating is structural, global and accelerating.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Tasks that took weeks now take hours, and soon minutes or seconds.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Change no longer moves in a linear way, it moves exponentially.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: In this context, adoption is no longer optional.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: In Singapore, while large firms wrestle with legacy systems and heavy compliance, and SMEs face severe constraints in capital and bandwidth, the implication is the same for both: enterprises that do not adopt AI will struggle to remain competitive.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: But if AI adoption is necessary, disruption is inevitable.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We must be clear about the risks to workers if this transition is not managed carefully.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: On one hand, as AI lowers the cost of many tasks, demand for those tasks can expand rather than contract.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Economists refer to this as the "Jevons employment effect", where efficiency leads not to less work, but to more work in new forms.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Word processors increased output and shifted work to higher-value roles.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: But the practical reality often produces a K-shaped outcome.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Experienced, AI-enabled workers capture disproportionate gains, while those without such capabilities, especially entry-level workers, risk falling behind.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: So, the question is not whether AI creates growth.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The real risk is not that AI replaces jobs.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It is that it replaces opportunity at scale.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: A worker may remain employed but face slower progression and a quiet erosion of experience.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It is not enough to observe whether firms adopt AI.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We must demand accountability for what happens after adoption.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Are workers better off after transformation than before it?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We must ask: are jobs and workflows being redesigned?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: If AI raises output but weakens livelihoods, that is not transformation.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: If public grants are funding a company’s pivot, should it not be explicitly tied to a national, human-centric scorecard?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: If we are serious about no jobless growth, our adoption metrics must move beyond counting jobs to measuring careers.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: From our work in AI fluency in Temasek, we know companies are urgently asking for guidance in leadership capability, job redesign, measurement of outcomes, trust and governance.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This is where our Labour Movement, NTUC, e2i and the unions come into play.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We must empower them to provide this guidance, ensuring that union leaders and management sit at the same table, mapping out the enterprises' technology roadmap and the workers' retraining schedules simultaneously.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: If companies need guidance on job redesign and shared outcomes, our tripartite partners must be right there on the ground with them.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The recently announced Tripartite Jobs Council is a timely step, but it must actively bridge the gap between firm-level transformation and worker-level outcomes.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Because the real challenge is not introducing AI into firms, it is integrating workers into that transformation.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This brings us to the central challenge of this transition: AI is not just a technology multiplier; it is a leadership multiplier.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Leaders must have real conviction in the transformational potential of AI and lead by example in using it, guiding its application and bringing their workforce along.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: But it cannot exercise judgement, build trust or carry people through uncertainty.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We are already seeing this tension play out globally.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We have seen Amazon announcing 16,000 job cuts in early 2026 while leaning further into AI for corporate efficiency.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: When AI is introduced mainly as a headcount strategy, it breeds fear.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: When introduced as a capability strategy, it builds trust.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Stories of this fear have long played out in our workplace, even among AI-enabled workers.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: When generative AI first started trending, some workers proactively explored AI on their own to improve their efficiency at work, but kept it a secret.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: They worry that if they reveal the source of their newfound productivity, they will eventually be made redundant or be loaded with more work without extra compensation.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: When trust is absent and gains are not shared, workers hide their capabilities rather than sharing them.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: True transformation requires leaders to adopt a long-term perspective.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Firms must expect short-term productivity lags as workers transition to new ways of working and they must create space for experimentation.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We ask workers to change, but we leave the system unchanged.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: AI cuts across functions and domains, reimagining how processes connect and how value is created.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: That reshaping of the entire process must come before individual roles themselves are redesigned.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: However, here lies a significant gap in our current policy approach.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Today, much of our national support is heavily focused on individual job redesign.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We ask workers to adapt to new job scopes, but legacy company processes are left unchanged.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: As a result, AI is often layered onto outdated workflows with silos and fragmented data.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: How can we provide enterprises with the expertise and funding to reimagine their cross-functional processes first?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: If we fix the workflow, workers will naturally see the value of the technology, turning inertia into eagerness to adapt.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Some workers will be displaced and some roles will change faster than expected.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We often point to existing measures like SkillsFuture and career conversion programmes.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: But here is a hard truth – if these measures are sufficient, why are our workers still so deeply anxious?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: For the workers who remain, basic AI capability will no longer be a distinct advantage.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It will be the price of staying in the game.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The task is to help workers transition from being mere AI users to becoming AI conductors, workers who know how to curate, steer and verify AI outputs.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This brings me to a critical concern regarding our workforce pipeline.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: If AI automates drafting, summarising and first-pass analysis, what happens to our entry-level jobs?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: In the Temasek ecosystem, we see companies investing in AI, piloting new tools and pushing forward with transformation.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: But the decisive constraint is not the technology.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: I shared this story with chief technology officers across our Temasek companies.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: But productivity fell, not because the technology failed, but because the people were left behind.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: On another line, the company did something different.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It was the capability and confidence of the people using it.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Workers who once feared change began to lead it.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: And in an AI transition, fluency, not just adoption, determines whether that direction is inclusive.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: That brings us to the Motion before us.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: An AI transition with no jobless growth is not just about creating jobs.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It is about ensuring that workers advance with technology, not fall behind it.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It is about turning innovation into shared outcomes.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: If adoption builds capability, then fluency must build advantage.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: If work is redesigned, then skills must be deepened.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: If growth is created, then it must be broadly shared.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: But this will not happen on its own.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: And this is where Singapore has a unique advantage.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Our model of tripartism, where Government, employers and workers move together, gives us the ability not just to react to change, but to shape it.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: When jobs are redesigned, workers must be involved.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Because this is not just a technology transition, it is a workforce transition.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: But we must be clear about the future we are building.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It cannot be one that says, "Stop having humans".

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It must be one that says, "Invest in people".

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Whether our workers advance is a choice we must make together, deliberately and decisively.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I argue that if our objective is to protect our workforce from job losses that could result from an economy-wide embrace of AI, then our efforts today should mainly be directed towards policies that promote new hiring rather than those that focus either on reducing displacement or pushing for retraining.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: In principle, the consequences of AI could bite on two ends of the labour market.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: It could reduce the incentives for firms to hire, thereby lowering the number of total new job openings, or it could raise the frequency of hiring by companies or induce workers to quit.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Hiring slowdown results when AI tools allow a company to cheaply and effectively replace job functions that they previously needed to hire a human worker for.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This is especially the case for entry level since the lack of experience among new graduates and the relatively straightforward grunt work new hires are generally tasked to do make this group somewhat less valuable and more replaceable by a machine.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But as many observers, including Members of this House, have already pointed out, this is a chicken and egg problem.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: If we do not absorb new workers into our corporations, we surely cannot expect them to gain the necessary experience and job-specific skills that make them valuable as mid-career professionals.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Job displacement occurs, in contrast, when AI tools reveal that certain roles are no longer needed as they can be well replicated by AI.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Tasks that used to be done by a human are replaced and if there is nowhere else in the firm for this person to be reassigned to or if the individual turns out to be too costly, then they are let go.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: On the positive side, AI could open up new opportunities for displaced workers to pursue a career elsewhere, either because they gain AI-related skills that make them more valuable in the marketplace or because perhaps they could go into business for themselves.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: For now, however, the message from studies worldwide is clear.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: While there has been little evidence of displacement thus far, there are more ample signs that there has been a decline in hiring.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This has been the case for AI-exposed sectors following the advent of generative AI such as ChatGPT and is likely to accelerate as agentic AI matures.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Prospects are especially perilous for early-career, entry-level workers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: And even when hired, such workers tend to receive lower salaries.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: AI mainly substitutes for mechanical, repeatable and well-defined tasks, which are mostly performed by junior employees.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Firms still value the maturity and experience of senior employees and, by and large, would rather skimp on hiring and re-allocate their otherwise loyal staff rather than giving them the boot.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Thus far, AI is yet to contribute much to job displacement here.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Moreover, Senior Parliamentary Secretary Huang also pointed to the large number of vacancies – around 10 times higher – in these sectors over the same period.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This could be interpreted as a healthy robust labour market for new hires, but I will caution against it.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This is because as any jobseeker will tell you – an opening does not a job make.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: These jobs have to be filled, ideally by Singaporeans who are themselves looking for jobs.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Here is where the picture is less encouraging.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: In response to a Parliamentary Question filed, Minister Desmond Lee pointed to how the decline was due to a post-pandemic hiring surge and that what we are seeing is simply a mean reversion to the early trend.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The youth unemployment rate which is lower in the 2020s then it was in the prior two decades has admittedly, elsewhere in the world, also steadily inched up since 2022, by around a percentage point.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: And unlike earlier instances when uptakes followed an economic cycle, Singapore's economy is actually currently in expansion.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: On the demand side there has also been reports that some employers have been tentative and reluctant to onboard workers, albeit these thankfully appear to be a minority for now.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Moreover, this pessimistic picture also mass more troubling pathologies.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Many Singaporean workers may have had to contend themselves with opportunities that do not fully employ their skills and talent.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Such mismatches are not well captured by the aggregate data.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Think of the graduate with an advanced degree from a local university but nevertheless still felt compelled to work in food delivery, or the student who spent years at a top university abroad but has been repeatedly rejected by employers since coming home.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Or the experienced mid-career professional with bills and a young family to support, who floundered unsuccessfully in the job market month after month despite upskilling as advised.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I believe others in this House will have seen cases similar to these in our weekly Meet-the-People Sessions.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: And indeed, two recent studies published by NTUC and MOM, corroborate these examples.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Coupled with the global climate of economic policy uncertainty, we may be heading toward an era of the so-called "great hesitation" in hiring in our local labour markets, similar to what has been observed elsewhere in the world.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: If our goal is, as the title of the Motion suggests, to avoid jobless growth, then it follows that we should prioritise policies that target the hiring of the labour market.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: First, we can improve the incentives for companies to hire fresh graduates.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Young workers will be free to apply their SkillsFuture credits toward paid apprenticeship and internship programmes with companies willing to take them on.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Corporations, especially SMEs, should also be able to submit credible proposals for in-house, on-the-job training to MOM, which will then offset the cost of taking on these trainees, drawing on the SkillsFuture enterprise credit and other subsidy schemes already earmarked for businesses.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: My hon friend, Gerald Giam, has also proposed an AI mastery fund for this purpose, which is complementary to what I am suggesting here.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Third, we can ramp up the delivery of social skills training in communication, empathy, judgement, networking and vision in the final year of their tertiary education prior to workforce entry.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Research has shown that AI is the most complementary to workers when the job demands require the fulfilment of not only cognitive tasks, but also in iterative collaboration between humans and AI.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But our graduates often load their school time with the pursuit of academic competencies, leaving them woefully under prepared for such interfacing functions.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This can occur with proof of skills via a series of micro credentials, or when candidates pass a live demonstration during the interview stage.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Like all general-purpose technologies before it, AI will destroy perhaps as many jobs as it creates, but as we confront the bleeding edge of this transition, we must set the stage for those who are most affected by the roll-out, which, for now, at least are clearly our young entry level workers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: We need targeted policies that will help sidestep the great hesitation in hiring them.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This is how we best ensure that the growth promises of AI are not overshadowed by fears of millions of missing jobs.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: AI is what we really call disruptive technologies, of which I spent my doctorate on.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: It is paradigm shift and when you say paradigm shift means it is shifting from one, or completely one industry to other areas that actually will destroy the old ways of working.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: Last week, I visited at AI startup in the Science Park, so we were talking about collaborations on a couple of projects in media, and I only saw two persons in the room with a capacity of 20 persons.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: So, I asked the chief executive officer, "Where are all the staff?" They say, well, they never come to the office, but they are working.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: And I say, "When do you see them?" They say, "Well, I saw them last week when the network went down and there were no communications.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: We can look at it from two angles: one is this company is supremely productive; the other thing to look at is, we have five jobs less.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: Well, if you are the CEO, you know what to choose.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: If you are the NTUC Secretary-General, I am not so sure.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: He happened to be interviewing potential staff for his expansion, and so I ask him, "How do you find this guy who is doing his Masters in computing?

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: Two years behind and I was like, wow, so when this guy graduates, maybe next year, what is going to happen to him?

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: Technology is always two years in front of him.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: And therefore, that means, do we put this guy into the real environment, which is basically internship, on-the-job attachments, or this person when he graduates, he really needs to speed up on the current competencies where the AI technologies are moving so fast.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: Personally, I get myself involved in the small little non-governmental organisations.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: We are working on one pet project, which is to monitor the senior citizens who are staying alone, so that if anything happens to them, we know.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: And we actually are using AI, because most of these senior citizens speak dialect dialects, so we are using robot companions, small ones, with the ability to understand dialects; and to monitor them.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
