text: It is very good, because it is very difficult to get caregivers to go around monitoring and visiting these people.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: So that is one thing that the AI is really, really useful for.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: The robotics AIs are really useful so that we can cover things that Singaporeans do not want or are probably not so suitable to do the job.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: The other projects that I am working on is imaging, using AI for magnetic resonance imaging.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: We will talk about it in some other time.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: The issue is that the workplace experience is now changing quite a bit.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: So, do we, or our staff, or our existing people, or PMEs, or workers have the skills for them to carry on in the job.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: I am glad actually that the Labour Movement has introduced the CTCs.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: It is a very good mechanism to bring AI into the workplace or working with the enterprise.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: And I am glad that there are such grants for it.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: But the question then is how do we define competencies?

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: Some Members talked about the workflow redesign, process redesign – but how do we know that at the end they are competent?

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: But what else can we do with these competencies?

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: And therefore, it is portable for this person throughout his careers.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: Like most workers, initially, I was, I would not say sceptical, but unwilling to change my style.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: But now, I think I have got no choice.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: So, for the past one year, I have been working on it.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: Even my wife has to use AI to generate videos and pictures, although she is an artist, she likes to draw – but it has become part of her life.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: It is a tsunami of change and I support the Motion.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: As I have previously done in my previous voluntary life as a council member of Institutions of Engineer, Singapore, I am the one who actually proposed working with the Labour Movement to set up the Young Engineers Leadership Programme, including the advanced and the global.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: I believe that the engineering institutions and the professional institutions could work with the labour unions to certify all such programmes for career pathways for the workers.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: (In Mandarin):   Mr Speaker, I agree with many of the points raised in the Motion, including the commitment to ensure that no worker is left behind during the AI transition.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, to realise this vision, we also need to share the gains from adopting AI and ensure that future workers can continue to remain competitive and stay ahead of the curve.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: When AI improves productivity and work efficiency, we should encourage workers to use the time freed up to be with their families, to rest, to participate in activities and to build relationships with others.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Additionally, the workers of tomorrow – who are the children in our schools today – are also already beginning to encounter AI in the classrooms.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Some parents have raised concerns about whether introducing AI to children at Primary 4 might be too early.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Neuroscientists have also pointed out that premature or excessive use of AI and technology may make learning too easy, thereby depriving children of the opportunity to develop deep learning capabilities.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In the AI era, independent thinking and judgement are the very skills that AI cannot replace.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: These are what we should be imparting to the next generation so that they remain competitive and resilient, no matter how the world changes. : Mr Speaker, I share the values outlined in the Motion: that growth must be inclusive, that every worker matters and that no one should be left behind in the AI transition.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Ensuring that no one is left behind involves more than just ensuring job full growth.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It requires a commitment to sharing the rewards of AI driven productivity.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It also requires that we ensure that future generations of workers can thrive in an era defined by AI and possibly other technologies have that have not yet been invented.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: While these efforts are essential, they do not answer another equally important question: how do we ensure that the equitable distribution of the AI productivity dividend?

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: They benefit from either more output from the same headcount or the same output from a lower headcount.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Such productivity gains do not automatically become employee gains.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Without deliberate policy design, they tend to remain exclusively employer gains.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: One way to share the AI productivity dividend with workers could be through time.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The right to request flexible work is not the same as the right to have it.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We should not rely on guidelines that place the burden of action on the employee who can least afford to do so.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It has become more salient as we discuss how the AI transition can benefit Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: As AI generates real productivity gains, the question of whether Singaporean workers will share in these gains as time regained, not just as higher output, is one which the market will not answer on its own.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It means the parents who can be present and do more than just paying for tuition classes.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: There are conditions under which human capabilities are replenished and sustained.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If so, I urge the Government to begin by giving legislative teeth to flexible work arrangements.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: As AI makes company more productive, workers should have a meaningful and enforceable claim on the time that AI frees up.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Time to rest and to pursue the kind of human connection that AI cannot replicate, and that our fertility rate is telling us we are running short of.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If we say that every worker matters, then we must look at the workers who are not yet in the workforce.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And I am talking about our children who are in today's classrooms and some of them in the galleries above.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Right now, our 10-year-olds in Primary 4 are being introduced to AI tools.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: While there is, of course, teacher supervision and guardrails in place, we should also be asking a more fundamental question.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Is this early exposure building their capability and ability to thrive in an AI world, or is it building an early dependence on AI-powered tools?

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: There are also serious questions being asked by neuroscientists.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In his book, "The Digital Delusion", neuroscientist Dr Jared Horvath makes a point that should give us pause.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: When technology makes thinking too easy, the depth of learning disappears.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It reads, writes and calculates with minimal user input.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But our children are not yet experts looking to offload and increase productivity.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It requires the cognitive friction that AI is designed to remove.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If our children start to offload their thinking at age 10, they do not develop the mental muscles needed to spot errors, ask meaningful questions, or form independent views.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: What we call AI-enabled personalised learning, then risks becoming customised comfort.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It feels like progress because it is frictionless, but it may be short circuiting the cognitive development we are trying to support.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This brings me to a concern that I raised earlier today: the equity paradox in AI use.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I appreciate Minister Desmond Lee's point about how MOE actively engages parents through Parents Gateway and share guidance on how they can better support their children at home.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But not every child in Singapore has a parent at home who is digitally engaged, has the time to act on that guidance and is equipped to scaffold their children's learning beyond what happens in a classroom.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Children from less privileged backgrounds with less access to parental guidance and fewer non-screen enrichment activities may end up leaning on AI more heavily, and not less.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For a child who comes home to an overstretched household where there is no one to redirect, question or supervise, AI will always produce an answer, always reduce the friction and always make the thinking easier.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If AI dependency erodes cognitive development that it is meant to supplement, then the children most at risk are the ones that we are trying our hardest to support.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: These abilities are built or not built over years.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If we displace that effort at age 10, our children cannot simply download it at university.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And if the children who are doing the most unsupervised AI offloading are those who already have less of these abilities, then we are not closing the gap.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I am suggesting that we follow the evidence, not the hype.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Generative AI has been public for barely four years.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We do not yet have long-term data on how it affects a child's brain.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We must ensure that we are preparing our children for a world we cannot predict by giving them the one tool that will always be relevant: a strong and independent mind.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This Motion rightly calls for Singapore's approach to AI enabled growth to be anchored in fairness, resilience and opportunity for all.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And this is why I spoke today about two critical things that the AI transition is challenging us to protect: time and mind.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And for our children, the workers of the future, we must protect the cognitive friction necessary for learning, ensuring that we are cultivating independent minds that can solve a hard problem without reaching for a digital crutch.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The AI transition is not just an economic event.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is perhaps the most significant opportunity in a generation for us to ask what kind of society we will build with the time and capability that technology returns to us.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: It is improving productivity, enabling new business models and strengthening our global competitiveness.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: But alongside these benefits, there is also a real concern – how do we ensure our workers are not displaced faster than they can adapt?

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Over the course of human history, economic growth has been corelated with the creation of new jobs.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: When countries moved through industrialisation for example, as industries opened, new jobs were created for people all around.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Of course, economic growth can also come not just from increases in labour, but also increases in productivity.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: And this is also to be welcome because it creates higher paying jobs for those who are working.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Singapore has benefited from both of these trends.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Against this backdrop, the conceptual concern with AI is a simple one: will it increase productivity so much that significantly fewer jobs will be needed?

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The implication for this is that the fewer people who have jobs or alternatively, those that control capital, will get all the benefits from the higher productivity while a large group of people will lose jobs.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Essentially, the winners will take a lot more and there will be a larger number of losers.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: If we look at developments in other countries, we see that governments are beginning to respond.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: They do so not by stopping technological change, but by introducing measured safeguards to ensure that workers are treated fairly as the adoption of AI increases.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: One area I wish to discuss is the use of AI in the job selection process itself.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: In an employment context, this means that important decisions, such as hiring or dismissal, cannot be made purely by algorithms without meaningful human involvement.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: While these are not laws which directly prevent job loss, they do ensure that decisions affecting employment are not made with reliance on AI in an opaque or unaccountable manner.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: They also promote fairness and help guard against unintended discrimination in automated decision-making.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Meanwhile, in countries such as Germany and France, labour laws require employers to follow structured processes before lay-offs, including consulting employee representatives, providing advance notice, and making efforts to retrain or redeploy workers.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Our NTUC is engaged in similar activities with our employers here.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: These requirements may not be specific to AI, but they help ensure that transitions are managed in a structured and responsible manner.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This is particularly important in maintaining trust between employers and workers.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: If workers feel that decisions are being made transparently and with safeguards in place, they are more likely to support rather than resist the adoption of new technologies.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: For Singapore, we can consider whether there should be clearer expectations around human oversight in employment decisions involving AI.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: While many employers already adopt such practices, formalising this principle can help ensure consistency across sectors.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: We can also explore whether workers should have a clearer right to transparency, including the right to know when AI systems are being used to assess their performance or influence decisions about their employment.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: In addition, it is worth considering whether we should strengthen expectations around responsible workforce transitions.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: When major technological changes significantly affect jobs, employers can be encouraged to provide structured support such as retraining opportunities or redeployment pathways.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Ultimately, it is important to recognise that legislation alone is insufficient and must be complemented by strong institutions, proactive employers and workers who are willing to adapt and learn.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Our goal should be to maintain a system where businesses remain innovative and competitive, workers feel secure and supported, and opportunities continuing to expand over time.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This leads me to my second point – what we can do for jobs which are most likely to be affected by AI.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: AI is particularly effective at performing routine and rules-based tasks.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: However, the issue is not simply that these jobs may disappear.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: More importantly, these roles often serve as entry points into the workforce, providing workers with the experience and skills needed to progress.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: If such opportunities are reduced, workers may find it harder to build careers over time.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: In this sense, the risk is not only displacement, but also the gradual erosion of career pathways.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Over time, this could lead to a situation where it becomes increasingly difficult for individuals to move from entry-level positions into more skilled and higher-paying roles.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Therefore, beyond retraining in a general sense, our focus should also be on facilitating practical transitions.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Workers should be supported in moving into adjacent roles where their existing skills can still be applied and built upon.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This makes transitions more feasible, particularly for mid-career workers.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: At the same time, companies can be encouraged to redesign jobs so that AI complements rather than replaces human workers.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: For example, while routine tasks can be automated, human roles requiring judgement, communication and problem-solving can and should be retained and enhanced.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This way, AI becomes a tool which increases productivity rather than a substitute for labour.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The unions, the Government and employers can work together on a framework for this.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This may include the right to one's image and voice.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Singapore has navigated many economic transitions successfully over the years.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Each time, we have combined openness to change with a commitment to social mobility and shared progress.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The transition to an AI-driven economy will be another such test.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: It will require us to strike a careful balance between innovation and protection.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: If we approach this thoughtfully, we can ensure that AI becomes a source of opportunity and that growth remains inclusive.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: First, we must protect the economic positions of workers and prevent the economic fruits of AI from accruing solely to those who own the AI models or produce the hardware powering AI.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: Second, we must ensure that AI-resilient employment pathways remain viable for Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: Third and most importantly, we must hold firm to the idea that technology should serve humanity and not the other way around, because ultimately, the goal is not just growth without joblessness.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: Screenshots will be taken occasionally throughout the workday.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: All this data will form datasets used to train AI systems that could one day replace these employees.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: While this is being done in the US, we in Singapore should ask whether companies such as Meta should be allowed to harvest employee data in this way without any clear safeguards.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: Should there not be stronger protections about how such data is collected and used?

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: Should workers not have a stake in the value that is created in their own data?

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: If we fail to address these questions, we risk sleepwalking into a future where wealth and power are concentrated in the hands of a few technology giants who increasingly use AI to take over work previously done by their human employees.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: These firms will continue to be the engine of economic growth, investing in larger and larger data centres and more powerful semiconductor chips that continue to generate gross domestic product growth.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: As a country, Singapore may benefit through our shareholdings in and partnerships with these tech companies.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: However, we must ensure that these benefits, which primarily accrue to the capital owners, do not come at the expense of the labour force.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: These developments pose a real risk that workers who are replaced may see their economic power steadily eroded, with a larger number of workers having to chase after a smaller pool of lower-paying jobs.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: I do not mean to be alarmist in suggesting that if unchecked, what could emerge is a form of digital serfdom, a system where workers like serfs of old are not bound by land or feudal lords but by algorithms.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: We are already seeing the beginnings of this future play out in real time.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: Already, platform workers work in service to black box algorithms that have a great deal of control over their earnings and how many hours they work.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: As AI advances, many cognitive and white-collar jobs will become increasingly automated and possibly, under the control of algorithms.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: Roles once considered secure may no longer be so.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: AI-enabled growth must not come at the cost of workers and a further tilting of the balance of economic power towards capital owners.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: Even as AI threatens to automate and replacement many existing roles, there remain many forms of labour that are difficult to automate using AI.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: For example, plumbers, electricians, air-conditioning technicians, phlebotomists and other skilled trades have been assessed to be much less likely to be replaced by AI.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: These jobs are essential pillars of a functioning society.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: Yet for too long, we in Singapore have undervalued these roles, both economically and socially.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: If we are serious about ensuring that growth remains inclusive, we must correct this imbalance.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: We must elevate their status not just through policy, but through culture and education so that Singaporeans will no longer see such jobs as undesirable.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: For example, should we recalibrate our policies in certain sectors to ensure that wages for local skilled trades rise meaningfully and attract more Singaporeans to fill these roles?

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: At the same time, we must make better use of our strong vocational institutions.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: Our ITEs and polytechnics should guide more students towards specialised high-value trades.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: In an AI-driven future, the dignity of work must not be tied solely to whether a job is white-collar or high tech.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: We must expand the range of jobs that Singaporeans considered attractive and meaningful.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: But we should not allow AI to come to define us as humans, as citizens and as Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: I say this because the question before us is not merely whether AI will create or destroy jobs.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: The deeper question is this: what kind of society and what kind of human beings will we become in an age shaped by AI?

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: Because Sir, if we are not careful, we may succeed economically, yet diminish ourselves in more fundamental ways.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: For example, AI has created a world where knowledge is no longer scarce.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: Texts can be summarised, essays can be written and equations can be solved in seconds.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: I spoke before about my own experience as an undergraduate struggling through dense text.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: It was slow, often frustrating work, but it was through that struggle that I learned how to think, how to question and how to make sense of the world.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: Today, however, the effort required to complete any cognitive activity has collapsed to an extent far greater than when the calculator replaced the abacus or the typewriter replaced the pen.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: The danger here is the temptation to use AI as a shortcut for thinking through and solving problems.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: On the one end, there are those who regard AI as a kind of second brain – outsourcing memory, decision-making and even aspects of judgement to ChatGPT or Claude.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: It is true that AI tools can sharpen our thinking and serve as intellectual aids.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: However, in creating a layer of artificial mediation between us and the world, I am concerned that AI would dull our capacity to make sense of the world.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: By making sense of the world, I mean the ability to interpret, comprehend and coherently perceive the world around us on our own terms, through our own cognitive efforts.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: And over time, this would involve reflective trial and error, balancing our considered interpretations and judgements of the world with how the world comes to bear upon us.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: Interpretation and judgement are practical skills that must be honed through constant and regular use.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: And we develop these skills by exercising, testing and challenging them.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: I am not against the idea of a second brain.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: My worry is more specific – that the reliance on a second brain, if left unchecked, will weaken the equity and reflexes of the first brain.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: On the other end, we see people forming emotional attachments with AI companions.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: These are relationships that stimulate empathy but do not truly reciprocate it.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: It demonstrates the real risk that people can lose sight of human relations in the real world.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: If people see these AI companions as a comforting shortcut to finding companionship in contrast to the hard work of developing friendships with others around us, we may see a further impoverishment of our social networks.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: In both cases, the danger is the same.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: We begin to substitute authentic human experience, sense-making and judgement with artificial approximations.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: And when that happens, we may gradually lose our ability to navigate the world with clarity on our own terms.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: There is a traditional Malay art form that is close to my heart: the pantun – a poetic form with its own specific rules.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: Made up of four lines, the pantun has a specific metre and rhyme scheme.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: Its imagery is typically drawn from nature and scenes of everyday life, to communicate important social values and advice.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: A pantun that does not follow these structures and conventions is usually not regarded as a good pantun, if it may be called one at all.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: Many pantuns are still known among Malays by heart, passed down orally through generations.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: Does the skill of using AI to generate pantuns necessarily translate into the craft of writing a good pantun, or even the aesthetic sensibility to appreciate the art form?

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: And what is the long-term impact to the Malay language, culture and tradition when a cultural motif is reduced to an AI output? : Sir, a final point.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: There is a traditional Malay art form that is close to my heart – the pantun.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: This is a poetic form with its own specific rules.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: Made up of four lines, a pantun has a specific meter and rhyme scheme.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: Imagery is usually drawn from nature and scenes of everyday life, to communicate important social values and advice.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: A pantun that does not follow these structures and conventions is usually not regarded as a good pantun, if it may be called one at all.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: Many pantuns are still known among Malays by heart, passed down orally through generations.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: In short, the pantun embodies a tradition, connecting the Malays today to our forefathers before.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: Hence, I want to ask: do we lose something valuable if we teach students to use AI to generate pantuns rather than the fun of experimenting with the lines themselves?

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: The Malays are cultured and courteous, the poets' inspiration will not be abandoned.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Sitting accordingly suspended at 3.51 pm until 4.10 pm.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Deputy Speaker, I declare my interest as a director of a company that makes AI-enabled applications and consults on the same.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: In the three and a half years since ChatGPT's release, I have had two moments of awe and dread.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: GPT-3.5 could iterate on software features, generate ideas, write code.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Five years ago, it was received wisdom that everyone should learn to code.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Computer science graduates, even from top schools, like Stanford, are finding it difficult to find jobs.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: GPT-2 was a toy that generated amusing limericks.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Three years later, its successors have made an entire profession's scarcity disappear.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: We used to talk about prompt engineering in 2023 and 2024.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: The second was in November 2025, when Anthropic released Claude Code, a reliable AI agent paired with a frontier model.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: I could leave the computer running overnight and there would be work done at the end.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: It is a different experience from chatting with a chatbot.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: The chatbot engages you in back and forth, refining your ideas, indulging your whims, red teaming your speeches.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: The agent, unless it needs clarifications, just goes and does things.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: It may be off by a bit, but you give your input and it takes another five or 50 minutes before it comes back with the problem solved.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Now we have AI agents, Claude Code, Codex tools, that have made me, if I may borrow Internet lingo, Claude-pilled.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: I use Claude Code for my own work.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: I can give it the most wishy-washy specifications, and it returns the most wonderful data workflow or website layout.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: For someone who could never build a pretty website to save his life, it is liberating.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: There is a spirit of play in working with these tools that every Singaporean deserves to experience.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: It is an exhausting world it heralds – software engineers pulling 80-hour weeks while running multiple AI agents overnight so that someone, human or machine, is always on the clock.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Jobseekers, especially recent graduates in white-collar work, applying to hundreds of jobs without a single interview.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Job portals, like LinkedIn, have become memory holds for resumes, where the lived experience is like shooting an application into the void.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: I am suspicious of any assertion that starts with "AI will never", because the shelf life of those predictions tend to be measured in months.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: What concerns me is not the destination, but who gets left behind on the way there and whether we are building the institutions to ensure no one does.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Second, that we must treat the handful of companies building frontier AI with the same strategic seriousness we bring to bilateral relations with countries, because their decisions on pricing, access and deployment now shape our productivity frontier as directly as any trade agreement.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Third, that we must buy time for workers by upgrading our retrenchment framework for AI-speed displacement.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Intelligence, in the sense of uplift, should not stratify according to wealth.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: I spend a couple of hundred dollars a month on these tools because they are game changing.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: But for those who cannot afford to, it bakes in inequality from the start.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Does it simply disqualify them from the off?

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: And critically, they likely will not cover AI agents – the tier where the real productivity gap will open.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: We may hope agent access follows the cost curve of Internet bandwidth or compute, but there is no necessary reason it should.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Anthropic's CEO said in January that 80% of its revenue comes from enterprise customers, driven by API calls on a pay-per-token model.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: If agents remain enterprise-grade by default, then individual citizens – jobseekers, freelancers, retirees – are locked out of the tier where the real productivity gains are being made.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: One, negotiate sovereign access – a bulk licensing agreement with frontier AI providers for volume-discounted AI agent access for all citizens.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Two, if agent access is employer-provisioned in the market, make it universally so, require companies above a certain size to provide agent-grade AI to all employees, the same way we require CPF.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Three, if frontier agents remain too costly, identify a minimal, viable agentic tier and fund that universally.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: And having just returned from China, I learned first-hand that one cannot use Claude Code there at all.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Anthropic blocks API calls from mainland China, Hong Kong and Macau entirely.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: If even engineers building frontier AI are desperate for access to one another's tools and if entire countries can be locked out, then access is not a convenience.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: And the question for our country is whether we will secure it or whether we will be price-takers forever.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: There are, perhaps, three to five companies in the world whose decisions on pricing, access and deployment will shape every economy's AI trajectory.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: When Anthropic or OpenAI decides what to charge for agent-tier access or whom to serve, that decision shapes Singapore's productivity frontier as directly as any trade agreement.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: We should therefore treat this class of companies – frontier AI firms that have crossed a threshold of systemic importance – with the same strategic seriousness that we bring to bilateral relations with countries.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Not because they are sovereign, they lack the durability and legitimacy of states and remain subject to home-state law, but because their decisions carry sovereign-grade consequences for our economy and we should engage them accordingly.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Second, we trade based on what we have.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has described the AI stack as a five-layer cake: energy, chips, infrastructure, models and applications.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: In my view, we do not have energy at scale.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: At the application layer, there is little moat outside of the knowledge agglomerations we can build for ourselves.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: We would be competing with some of the highest cost bases in the world.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: And we are among the world's leaders in water reuse and integrated water management, which is a binding constraint on data centre expansion across water-scarce regions in Southeast Asia.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: If we position ourselves as the infrastructure partner of choice for this region, that is real leverage – something we can bring to the table in exchange for access, for pricing and for presence.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: So, when a company like Anthropic or OpenAI approaches us, we should be their preferred regional bilateral partner in rolling out and scaling their data centre build-up regionally, as well as all the infrastructure needed to make these data centres work.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Third, we need to attract real technological presence.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: We should seek frontier AI companies establishing development offices here – not predominantly sales offices, which was the experience with the FAANG companies in the 2010s.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: And I would prefer that we be quality-conscious.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Most companies that call themselves "AI companies" are not frontier AI companies.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: We need targeted strategy and engagement with frontier AI companies specifically.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Once you are in the frontier AI ecosystem, it becomes much easier to circulate within that group of companies.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: I would welcome the Government doing some fact-finding – engaging our local and overseas Singaporeans already in these companies and roles, understanding how they or their colleagues got hired and disseminating that to our students and technical researchers.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Right now, anecdotally, half a million to million-US-dollar salaries, excluding equity, in the US for AI researchers are fairly common.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: So, it is clearly in our interest to figure out how to get more Singaporeans into this tight labour market.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: What I would really like to see is a Skills Framework for frontier AI lab researcher.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: In Hangzhou, a quality assurance supervisor named Zhou joined a tech company in late 2022 at RMB25,000 a month, about S$4,800, reviewing AI model outputs for accuracy and safety.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: In 2025, his employer decided an AI model could do his job.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: They offered him a reassignment at roughly 40% less pay.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: The company appealed and lost again, at the Hangzhou Intermediate People's Court.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: The ruling was published on 28 April this year, three days before International Workers' Day.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: The company argued that AI had made Zhou's role obsolete – a "major change in objective circumstances", justifying dismissal under China's Labor Contract Law.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: AI adoption, it held, is a deliberate business strategy, not an unforeseeable event.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: A company that chooses to automate cannot unilaterally shift the full cost of that decision onto the worker.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: The company had not shown the contract was impossible to perform and the reassignment at 40% less pay was not a reasonable alternative.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: The court added that companies should prioritise retraining workers and helping them transition to higher-level roles.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: The principle, that a deliberate business decision should not externalise its full cost onto the worker, deserves serious consideration in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: If a Singaporean Zhou were retrenched tomorrow under our existing framework, would he win?

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Our existing Tripartite Advisory on Managing Excess Manpower and Responsible Retrenchment (TAMEM) is advisory, not statutory.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: An employer can lawfully automate a role and terminate the worker without first attempting to redeploy or reskill them.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: And the public purse, through SkillsFuture and Workforce Singapore, would pick up the cost of that worker's transition.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: There is no individual cause of action for the worker to challenge the reason for his or her termination.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: The data suggests we are entering the zone where this matters.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Retrenchments were concentrated in Financial Services, Information and Communications, and Professional Services – the most AI-exposed sectors.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Information and Communications employment declined outright in 2025.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: But it creates no new powers, no new obligations on employers and no new rights for displaced workers.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: How does the Government intend for this Council to work?

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Too often, what workers experience is not a frank conversation about AI-driven restructuring but a Performance Improvement Plan, a process that, in many cases, is a bit of "wayang", designed to paper over a predetermined outcome.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: I foresee that such potential misleading reasons may be given and workers must have the power to be able to challenge this.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: These provisions will slow the velocity of AI disruption; and velocity is what determines whether adjustment is possible.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: They were happier, less stressed – and the great majority still walked into the employment office and asked for work.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: People, when offered the choice between a universal basic income and employment, invariably choose employment.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Not because they are irrational, but because a job is where you are needed, and being needed is not something a universal basic income can replace.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: But more than that: no growth where the gains are captured disproportionately by capital and the burden of adjustment falls on labour.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Universal access, so intelligence is not rationed by wealth.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: I do not think the awe and dread goes away.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: But in a country that builds for its workers, there is hope for a brighter future.

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari (Nominated Member)
text: With all the discussions so far, there is no doubt that AI brings about new opportunities, new tools, new ways of working and the potential for better jobs.

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari (Nominated Member)
text: For the Labour Movement, an AI transition with no jobless growth must means three things.

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari (Nominated Member)
text: First, AI augments workers, it does not replace them wholesale.

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari (Nominated Member)
text: Two, the productivity gains from AI are reinvested into people, into training, into new industries, into better wages and real growth.

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari (Nominated Member)
text: Three, no worker is left to navigate this transition alone.

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari (Nominated Member)
text: I will speak to each of these in turn.

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari (Nominated Member)
text: They will tend to concentrate in firms with the scale and capability to deploy it.

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari (Nominated Member)
text: The business case for transformation is compelling and I support the Government's announced efforts to support enterprises on this to accelerate their AI adoption, so that they can seize new opportunities.

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari (Nominated Member)
text: However, I call on businesses seeking to grow their pie, to be laser-focused on job redesign and training to bring their workers along with them.

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari (Nominated Member)
text: Here, I must appreciate the many hon Members who have supported this call.

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari (Nominated Member)
text: Globally, there are warnings that AI could significantly reduce entry-level white-collar roles in the coming years.

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari (Nominated Member)
text: While firms rationalise their workforce sizes and skills mix, we must be clear-minded that not all of such rationalisation may translate into economic growth that enables our families to thrive, children to flourish and seniors to enjoy their golden years.

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari (Nominated Member)
text: They want to know that there are pathways for the gains from AI to benefit workers, and not just management and shareholders.

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari (Nominated Member)
text: Many workplaces are only at the beginning of figuring out what such pathways need to look like and the pitfalls of failing to provide such pathways.

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari (Nominated Member)
text: As mentioned by some Members, recently, courts in China have been active in reviewing cases regarding the dismissal of employees due to AI-related restructuring and choosing to protect labour rights against unfair AI-related lay-offs.

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari (Nominated Member)
text: It must work with the unions through the CTCs or the tripartite frameworks, to ensure this is managed together.

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari (Nominated Member)
text: We should make this a baseline, and not the exception.

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari (Nominated Member)
text: The social contract between employer and employee must evolve alongside technology.

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari (Nominated Member)
text: Unions should be involved early in the company's transition plans to integrate new technology, implement job redesign and transition workers to handle new work.

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari (Nominated Member)
text: In roles that AI is not displacing, AI is increasing the speed, density and complexity of work rather than reducing it.

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari (Nominated Member)
text: However, I caution that when AI has pushed human boundaries and job redesign is not done adequately in tandem, there is concern that the working environment will be unsustainable, with very high intensity and pressures that can lead to burn-out, fatigue and poorer psychosocial health.

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari (Nominated Member)
text: We already see this in many of today's workplaces, especially for PMEs, where work is increasingly outcome-based and the boundaries between work and personal life are more blurred.

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari (Nominated Member)
text: The psychosocial implications of AI enablement deserve further attention too.

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari (Nominated Member)
text: Our time-based employment protections were designed for a less digitally connected era with more fixed working hours and clearer boundaries.

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari (Nominated Member)
text: Today, these new emerging work patterns suggest there is room to further evolve how we can support workers.

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari (Nominated Member)
text: This is where our unions in Singapore play a critical role.

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari (Nominated Member)
text: Through collective agreements, company-level engagements and multi-company initiatives, such as the Queen Bee partnerships for the NTUC's CTC initiative, unions ensure that productivity gains are translated into better jobs, better wages and most importantly better working conditions, not just higher output and shareholder returns.

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari (Nominated Member)
text: In addition, when AI is deployed to support hiring decisions and performance reviews, we must watch for unintended biases and ensure safeguards for the confidentiality of information.

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari (Nominated Member)
text: Even when gains are shared, there is a harder question we must confront: what happens to workers whose jobs are displaced altogether?

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari (Nominated Member)
text: That advice assumes that workers have time, the financial buffer and margin for error to take such risks.

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari (Nominated Member)
text: I want to be honest, because vague optimism is a luxury that the displaced cannot afford and we must make sure the system watches for this.

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari (Nominated Member)
text: This is especially so for our mid-career and older PMEs.

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari (Nominated Member)
text: They are workers with mortgages and bills to pay, with children still in school and often, elderly parents to take care of.

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari (Nominated Member)
text: A failed transition is not just a momentary setback.

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari (Nominated Member)
text: This is where we must go further to support our breadwinners and their families, ensuring that reskilling leads to real job outcomes, that transitions are supported and that pathways to good jobs are clear, especially for those making mid-career shifts.

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari (Nominated Member)
text: And instead of minimum wages, progressive wage models for key segments of our workforce.

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari (Nominated Member)
text: For the AI era, we can seek better support for our PME jobseekers.

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari (Nominated Member)
text: We must continue close monitoring of those who applied for jobseeker support and help them bounce back as soon as possible for the next better job.

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari (Nominated Member)
text: Giving workers a genuine voice in how AI enters their workforces is equally important.

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari (Nominated Member)
text: Across advanced economies, one principle is becoming clear, worker voice must be part of how technology reshapes work.

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari (Nominated Member)
text: In countries, like Belgium, unions and employers are already working together to establish norms around after-hours communication, workload and staffing.

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari (Nominated Member)
text: In Singapore, we have a strong foundation in our tripartite model.

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari (Nominated Member)
text: But as a unionist, I want to make a broader point.

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari (Nominated Member)
text: If we are serious about ensuring AI is used fairly and that the gains from AI-driven transformation reach workers, then we must welcome unions to represent PMEs who are most vulnerable in the AI era.

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari (Nominated Member)
text: PMEs are not a monolithic group – an engineer in aerospace, a financial analyst in banking, a project manager in the tech phase – very different work environments and go through very different impacts of AI transformations.

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari (Nominated Member)
text: Unions are able to shape workplace norms from ground up, in a targeted manner that recognises diversity.

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari (Nominated Member)
text: Hence, employers should consider allowing unions to represent PMEs.

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari (Nominated Member)
text: The mechanism for having the workers voice at the table is already here – it is the CTC.

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari (Nominated Member)
text: Through the CTC, unions work directly with management to chart out transformation roadmaps, redesign jobs and upskill workers so that no one is left behind when a company transforms.

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari (Nominated Member)
text: Such examples must be amplified and more employers should do such things.

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari (Nominated Member)
text: We must continue to leverage this to support workers and enterprises in the AI transition.

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari (Nominated Member)
text: I hope more leading multinational corporations can work with our unions to provide more training and uplift the AI skills of workers for our collective future.

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari (Nominated Member)
text: First, on sharing gains, we must ensure that as enterprises transform with AI, the gains are shared with workers through fair wages, better working conditions and clearer norms around work intensity, including expectations on after working hours communication and responsiveness.

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari (Nominated Member)
text: They must be calibrated to our Singapore context but clear in intent.

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari (Nominated Member)
text: Second, in supporting transitions, we must strengthen how we support workers through the AI transition by ensuring that AI enables enterprises to unlock new growth, that training leads to real job opportunities, that reskilling is twinned with job redesign and that workers are not left to navigate these changes on their own.

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari (Nominated Member)
text: Third, in giving workers voice, workers and their unions must be engaged early when AI is introduced into workplaces.

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari (Nominated Member)
text: Not just on hiring and other employment decisions, but on how AI changes job scopes, workflows and performance expectations.

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari (Nominated Member)
text: This means welcoming unions' ability to represent PMEs, and scaling mechanisms, like the CTC, so that worker voice is embedded in every transformation journey.

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari (Nominated Member)
text: An AI transition with no jobless growth is not a slogan.

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari (Nominated Member)
text: A commitment that growth should mean something to everyone, not just those at the top of the economic pyramid.

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari (Nominated Member)
text: But to the nurse, the teacher, the logistics worker, the small business owner, the young person entering the workforce for the very first time.

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari (Nominated Member)
text: They are not footnotes in the story of technological progress.

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari (Nominated Member)
text: They are the reason progress should matter at all.

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari (Nominated Member)
text: These are not competing priorities; they go hand-in-hand and we are standing at one of those rare inflection points in history where choices we make today will echo for the next generations.

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari (Nominated Member)
text: That is where the tripartite partners must deliver, must make this happen and that is also what I hope this House will help us deliver.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: I grew up in a very ordinary Singaporean home with working class parents, but was given an extraordinary opportunity to build and retrofit advanced factories across the world.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: From Germany to the United Kingdom, from North America to Asia, I have had the privilege of building and working on industry 4.0 facilities, cutting edge factories equipped with some of the most sophisticated machines ever created, machines that produce components of such precision that they can only be manufactured in a handful of places in the world and facilities that assembled some of the most advanced engineering systems ever built.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: It is not the machine, nor the technology that determines success.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: I have seen factories with the best technology money can buy struggle because of misalignment, because of distrust, because workers, unions, management and government were not moving in the same direction.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: And I have seen more modest facilities outperform expectations because everyone was aligned to a common purpose.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: That is why this debate matters, because when we talk about transformation, especially one driven by AI, we are not just talking about technology.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: We are talking about people, about workers, about livelihoods, about dignity.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: And I want to acknowledge our Labour Movement, NTUC Secretary-General, Mr Ng Chee Meng, and Ms Yeo Wan Ling and Members of this House, Mr Mark Lee and Mr Saktiandi Supaat, for putting forth this Motion.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: It is timely because it complements the direction set out by Prime Minister Mr Lawrence Wong in his Budget speech and the May Day Rally, where he spoke about how Singapore must confront the realities of AI and global uncertainty while standing firmly with our workers.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: And even as technology reshapes our economy, we must not leave our people behind.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Our Labour Movement has echoed this with clarity and conviction.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: That this transition must drive Singapore's next phase of growth, but it must be anchored in fairness and opportunity for all.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: We must equip both workers and enterprises to seize new opportunities so that progress is not just created but shared.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: This is the promise we must make to our next generation.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: And often to protect the jobs of today, they invariably have to resist change, even when the tide of change is inevitable.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: But what we have in Singapore is different.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: And our union leaders, like brother Samad from the Union of Power and Gas Employees, brother Fahmi from United Workers of Electronics and Electrical Industries, brother Poobalan and Goviden from SATS Workers' Union, brother Gabriel from the Amalgamated Union of Statutory Board Employees and many of our union leaders here, stand with the workers, not just for where they are today, but for where they need to be tomorrow.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: They focus on keeping workers relevant, employable and ready to take on better opportunities as the economy evolves.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: And that, Mr Deputy Speaker, is something that we should never take for granted.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Allow me to frame my position on the motion around three key ideas: transformative power, opportunity for all and jobless growth.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: The impact of AI can be understood at three levels, the individual, the enterprise and the industry.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: And at every level, success depends on how well workers, businesses and Government work together.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Many of us are already experiencing this today through tools, like Open AI, ChatGPT, Microsoft Copilot, Claude, Gemini and Canva, but this transformation does not happen by chance.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Workers must be prepared to learn, adapt and continuously upgrade themselves, and businesses must invest in training, redesign jobs and empower their workforce to use these tools effectively.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: It must remain accessible to the masses so that every worker has the opportunity to improve productivity, strengthen capabilities and participate meaningfully in Singapore's next phase of growth.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: At the level of the enterprise, AI enables better decision, sharper operations and greater efficiency.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: It turns data into insights and insights into action.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: But to realise this, companies need the right framework.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Workers need the right capabilities and the Government must provide the right environment to scale transformation responsibly.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: At the level of the industry, AI creates entirely new value.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: And speaking from my own experience in the industry, the decision to adopt AI is really just about tax incentives, as characterised by Member Mr Andre Low.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Very often, AI adoption is not a binary choice between technology and workers.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: It is about re-engineering business processes so that enterprises can do more with a more capable, more skilled and more productive workforce to take on the challenges of the world.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: These values, unlocked by AI, must be shared – shared so that workers are uplifted, businesses grow stronger and society moves forward together.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: But ultimately, this is a social compact we must continue to uphold between workers, businesses and government – one anchored on fairness, inclusion and shared progress.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Taken together, AI is not just any other technology tool.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: That is why tripartism matters even more in the age of AI.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: And I am heartened to hear the position of the Labour Movement.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: But it is also a period of real uncertainty.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: At what point do we ask whether this becomes a substitute for proper employment?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: As AI reshapes professions from developers to lawyers, how do we ensure there are still meaningful entry points for our young people?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: If companies begin to question entry-level roles, then we must also ask, who will train the next generation of our workforce?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Our mid-career workers feel this even more deeply.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: With families and responsibilities, they worry that job transformation may render their experience less relevant.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Our blue-collar workers – our technicians, our operators and drivers – are asking hard questions about automation and the future of their jobs.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: If left unaddressed, they can divide our society.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: That is why this opportunity for all cannot be left to market forces alone, a point also raised by Member Poh Li San.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: It requires companies and especially middle managers to give fresh graduates a real chance.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: It requires businesses to redesign jobs and invest honestly in upskilling and reskilling.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: It requires all of us to work together so that every Singaporean can find their place in this new economy.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Only then can we say that this is not just growth, but opportunity for all.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: In many economies, jobless growth means growth without jobs.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: So, this is not just about creating more jobs.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: It is about ensuring our people can take on the jobs that are created.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Avoiding this means focusing on capability, not just capacity.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: The Government must support hope with strong systems and pathways.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: When we do this well, growth will not leave people behind.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: My Deputy Speaker, in Malay, please. :   Mr Speaker, the discussion about AI today is no longer something distant from our lives.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: In Singapore and around the world, one thing is clear – AI brings hope, but also concern.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Within our Malay/Muslim community, these concerns are real.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Young people worry about the future of employment and whether opportunities still exist for them.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Those in mid-career are anxious about whether their experience and skills remain relevant.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: And blue-collar workers – including drivers, technicians and general workers – wonder whether their jobs will be replaced by automation.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: But at the same time, we cannot view AI only as a threat.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: We must see it as an opportunity – an opportunity to progress together.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Allow me to touch on three important points in the AI transformation.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: First, on building skills to be part of this transformative force.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: AI will only become a force multiplier if we know how to use it.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: At M3+ Pasir Ris–Changi, for example, we run various programmes to help the community enhance their skills and employment opportunities.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: These include Women-at-Work to help women return to the workforce, as well as the Career Marketplace held in Pasir Ris to open access to career opportunities and employment networks.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: It is an effort to build confidence, exposure and future-ready skills from a young age.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Regarding skills, the fear of AI should not prevent us from learning how to use it wisely.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: The concern that AI could diminish any deep understanding of the Malay language and culture, as well as other skills, is understandable – if it is used without understanding the basics and its limitations.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Like any other tool, what matters is how we use it.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Mastery of and appreciation for the Malay language remains key in understanding its beauty, values, and meaning.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: However, if used appropriately, AI can also help preserve our heritage.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Even classic Malay films can be preserved for future generations.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: If used wisely, AI can help preserve the language, strengthen culture and carry Malay heritage into the future with confidence.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Golden bananas brought to sea, One ripens atop a chest, If AI is used very wisely, Culture is inherited, in the heart it rests.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: AI, as we know, is a transformative technology.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: All of us recognise that it will profoundly transform business models across the economy and with it, the content and nature of work.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: As a small, open and technologically advanced nation, Singapore must strive to be at the forefront of new technologies, especially one as significant as AI.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: In addition to being critical for our economy, AI also has considerable potential to help address Singapore's demographic and societal challenges.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: But whether we embrace AI or fear it, there is no escaping the impact it will have on our companies and workforce.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: I will make four points in my speech.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: First, jobless growth is not an option for Singapore as good jobs are integral to inclusive growth and to a fair and vibrant society.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: Singapore's social compact is based on self-reliance through work.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: This means providing for oneself and one's family through employment and income.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: It has been said before in this House many years ago that "a job is the best welfare, and full employment is the best protection for the workers of Singapore." In this social contract, the Government's role is to nurture a pro-enterprise business environment conducive to investment and job creation.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: Any Singaporean who is willing to work hard will have enough to meet his or her housing, healthcare and retirement needs through CPF savings.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: In practice, significant Government support is given in the form of housing grants, CPF top-ups and healthcare subsidies to support home ownership, retirement adequacy and healthcare assurance.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: We now have more extensive risk pooling through social insurance, complementing individual savings in meeting healthcare and long-term care needs.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: Yet employment and income remain central to Singapore's socioeconomic model and social compact.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: Recent advances in AI pose a challenge to this model.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: Globally renowned AI pioneers and industry leaders have warned of the possibility of mass job displacements arising from AI.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: Predictions of a so-called "white collar bloodbath" or a "jobs apocalypse" have stoked public fear even as other commentators have asserted that these fears are overwrought.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: Transformative technologies in the past have indeed eliminated certain jobs, but they have created new jobs as well so that we are not all without jobs or leading lives of unlimited leisure.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: Generative AI has raised particular concern because it can take over jobs and tasks associated with human skill and creativity, including cognitive tasks such as coding and data analysis and creative tasks such as writing and design.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: These tasks require skills built through years of education and training and are consequently well remunerated.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: They underpin many of the good jobs that Singaporeans aspire to.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: While we should not underestimate the disruption from AI, there is still time to adapt and respond.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: Indeed, many Members of this House have pointed to this concern.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: This may be because the adoption of AI is still in its early stages for many companies here.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: It takes time for more firms to move from viewing AI as a mere project or productivity enhancement tool to fundamentally re-organising work processes around it.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: As the pace of AI adoption picks up, however, the benefits to firm productivity and profits will grow, but so too will the impact on jobs.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
