text: While we must consider the need for greater social support and new channels of redistribution to keep our society inclusive, we must also continue to equip citizens to provide for themselves through good jobs and incomes.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: Some of us may remember what President Tharman explained in an interview in 2015 at the St Gallen Symposium.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: He was describing Singapore’s approach, and I quote: "It is about keeping alive a culture where I feel proud that I own my home and I earn my own success through my job.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: I feel proud that I’m raising my family.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: And keeping that culture going is what keeps a society vibrant." If we look around the world at how economies have developed, it is clear that the key to success is the emergence of a strong middle class enabled by education and job creation.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: Many countries with large natural resource endowments have not done well, because their focus has been on resource extraction, benefiting the few, rather than education and skills development, which benefit the many.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: It is also evident that Singapore succeeded precisely because people are our only resource.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: This brings me to my second point, which is that we must support workers to develop deep domain knowledge, learning agility and career resilience.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: To equip workers for the AI age, training in AI tools is certainly important.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: Familiarity with AI and understanding of the strengths and limitations of different AI tools comes with frequent use, tinkering and experimentation.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: But that, as many in this House have also realised, is only part of the answer.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: After all, AI tools are supposed to become more intuitive and easier to use over time.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: The real value that people bring to jobs lies in deep understanding of domains or subject matter, which means all of us still have to put in the hard yards to learn and avoid "cognitive offloading" by creating productive friction in the learning process, whether in schools or at the workplace.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: AI can provide the scaffolding and can help personalise learning, but it must not become a substitute for thinking.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: The key skill that many have identified is learning how to learn, being adaptable and resilient to changes.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: The Singapore Opportunity Index developed by MOM highlights how employers can create opportunities for their workers such as through recruitment practices, career development pathways and job design.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: By identifying employers with a good track record of supporting career growth, employers will hopefully be encouraged to invest in their workers and help them chart their careers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: The third point I would like to bring up is that we must not only upskill workers for jobs, but also upgrade jobs for workers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: As I mentioned in my speech at MOM’s Committee of Supply debate, there will continue to be strong demand for workers in areas such as healthcare and skilled trades, driven by an ageing population and the relative resilience of these roles to AI displacement.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: However, such jobs have difficulty attracting Singaporeans as they are perceived to be less prestigious or rewarding, or perhaps less comfortable compared with white-collar office jobs.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: But the risk is that Singapore will become increasingly dependent on foreigners to take on essential work even as Singaporeans struggle to find jobs that meet their aspirations.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: Jobs and occupations that have traditionally been regarded as non-degree jobs therefore have to be redesigned to be suitable for a broad range of workers, including graduates.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: The jobs have to be redesigned to tap on workers' "head, heart and hand" skills, so that they are more engaging for workers and more resilient to AI disruption.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: This may involve taking on greater professional responsibility, increasing the cognitive, analytical and innovation content of jobs, and creating more opportunities for interpersonal engagement in the jobs.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: AI tools can in fact support the upgrading of vocational and semi-skilled jobs by augmenting human expertise.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: By making the whole range of these jobs attractive to Singaporeans, we can avoid structural overqualification or underemployment.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: My fourth point is that Singapore should build up expertise as a global reference point for skills-first and human-centric job redesign.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: A skills-first approach means that workers are not pigeonholed by formal qualifications into certain jobs or occupations.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: Employers recognise that workers, regardless of their starting point, can upskill to meet job requirements.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: Likewise, the scope of jobs and occupations can expand to make fuller use of workers' skills.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: AI is already fractionalising jobs – breaking them down into tasks, some of which are assigned to AI and others to human workers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: It is important for job redesign to be human centric so that human workers can still make a valuable contribution, augmented by AI and technology, rather than have processes entirely automated with minimal human involvement.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: With agentic AI now able to execute processes that span multiple job roles, it is no longer enough to redesign tasks within a particular job.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: Instead, organisations must look at redesigning end-to-end work processes.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: This is a capability that must be embedded within organisations as AI continually reshapes the nature of work.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: They attracted much international attention, with participation from experts, policy-makers and industry practitioners around the world.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: The impact of AI on work and learning is an issue that all countries and societies are grappling with, and no one has all the answers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: It is a fertile area of research as firms and societies seek to adapt and transform.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: We are in a complex operating environment with no tried-and-tested playbook to fall back on.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: As one corporate leader I spoke with recently put it: we are learning and adapting mid-flight.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: Both learning and job redesign in the age of AI must be iterative and experimental.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: We need the best minds in Singapore and around the world focused on this.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: Just as Singapore has world-leading research centres in new technologies like quantum computing, we should build up expertise and experience in adult learning and human-centric job redesign.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: Today, there are nodes of excellence across the institutes of higher learning.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: For instance, the polytechnics and ITE are among the national centres of excellence for workplace learning.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: Together, we can build up Singapore as a thought leader and living laboratory in the areas of adult learning, career health, human-AI complementarity and skills-first practices.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: As a global innovator plugged into international networks of cutting-edge research and practice, Singapore can help to shape the future of work in a way that supports both economic growth as well as human flourishing.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: This is important because it can no longer be taken for granted that economic growth in the future will be accompanied by full employment and rising incomes.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: Beyond adapting to AI, our end goal must be to enable every worker to grow, to contribute and to find meaning in work.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: It is a whole-of-nation effort where everyone has a part to play.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: Recently, an American journalist approached me to find out how Singapore is addressing AI and its impact on jobs.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: She noted that many major US corporations are under pressure to slash headcounts to boost profits.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: Indeed, there are expectations from shareholders and investors that management will replace workers with AI.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: With our unique tripartite collaboration and the commitment of all partners, I believe that companies and workers can approach the coming AI transition with resolve and confidence.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: I recall the first time at work when I received a draft legal submission from my younger colleague who had some content generated by AI, the alarm bells went off in my mind. "Is the content reliable?

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: Am I going to be taken to task by the Court for submitting this?" I was anxious and worried even though the content had been verified and put together with considered "human"-generated legal analysis.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: This incident made me recollect what happened when I first joined the legal profession.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: I would find written memos on my desk with instructions on matters from a particular Senior Partner.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: When I asked once, whether an email might be easier, I was told that an email was not reliable and that with a written memo, he was assured that I would receive the message.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: We all know better than to argue with our bosses but eventually, the written memos did move onto become emails, perhaps with the realisation that the email instructions would reliably reach me, even after office hours.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: As with each industrial and technological transformation in history, be it the steam engine, electricity, digitalisation with personal computers, connectivity with the Internet and now AI, change and transition always bring with them anxiety and the fear of the unknown.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: Humans are wired to be untrusting of that which we cannot control – and maybe even rightly so.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: With AI, we feel this acutely in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: Many Members in the House have spoken about these concerns and the anxieties felt by Singaporeans from all walks of life.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: As the adage goes, "change is the only constant".

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: Fear of the unknown is a natural reaction, but we should use it as a galvanising force to re-think old ways, learn new ones and as a result, seize new opportunities and grow.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: It recognises that harnessing AI to grow, is a double-edged sword.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: On the one hand, while AI can be a driver for the next phase of Singapore’s economic development; on the other, if its development and deployment is left unfettered, it can lead to societal ills such as job displacement and widening inequality.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: As the Prime Minister pointed out during his Budget Statement, AI is but a "tool".

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: How we harness it and manage its deployment will shape our economy, our jobs, our lives.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: Our approach to AI-enabled growth, as the Motion states, therefore, must be anchored in fairness, resilience and opportunities for all.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: The Motion resonates because it is about putting people at the centre of Singapore's approach to AI-enabled growth.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: Growth must be inclusive and benefit our people.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: We cannot have jobless growth at all costs.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: The anxieties and concerns of our workers and PMEs across industries are not hypothetical.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: Our young graduates entering the workforce for the first time face a daunting reality.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: As AI automates routine execution, employers are raising the bar, demanding higher-order critical thinking and AI collaboration skills from the outset.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: Left on its own, the AI disruption could very well lead to unfair outcomes.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: Organisations and individuals who manage a head-start or transition well, will benefit exponentially, while those who do not, will be left behind.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: However, AI fluency and literacy among the general population is also equally important.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: On this I would like to raise two points.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: First, you will recollect my personal anecdote at the start of my speech.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: Fluency with any tool, be it computers or smart phones in the past or AI today, is about building confidence.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: Mr Lim Boon Heng, a former NTUC Secretary-General shared with me, his experience with the Government's computerisation efforts in the 1980s.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: It was a strategic decision at the time, but workers were afraid of computers.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: So, the Government designed computer appreciation courses that were rolled out by the NTUC, using early Apple computers.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: Familiarisation with the use of the keyboard and for those who remember, playing games like PacMan.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: Workers slowly got past the fear and embraced the familiarity.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: Importantly, the key message must be, this is a tool that can help you do a job, better, faster.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: While it is vital that we upskill our workers to leverage on the AI tools that are relevant for their respective workplaces, AI fluency and literacy should be a national endeavour that is available in our schools, our Community Clubs and even our Active Ageing Centres.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: The idea is to embed AI fluency and literacy as a part of life, be it in creating a simple e-greeting card with an AI tool that creates moving graphics or building a billion-dollar company using bots.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: Only then can we envision an entire people advancing collectively together in an economy with AI-enabled growth.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: Second, supporting workers to become AI fluent should be more than just providing them with the AI tools and the know-how on using them.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: We must also equip and afford workers the time and ability to learn how to apply the AI tools in their workplaces.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: Getting young graduates past the door, and securing older workers and PMEs in new roles are imperative, but if AI is to transform our economy, we must ensure that our workforce learns effectively through deeper learning while persuading our businesses and organisations to create workplaces and systems that allow our workers to test their new skills, learn from mistakes and improve.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: At its broadest and most pervasive use as a tool, AI can generate content, summarise and answer in seconds.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: We need a workforce that not only can use the AI tool to obtain these outcomes, but to work with AI as a collaborative partner while applying judgment, reason, creativity and context to drive high-impact value – the human elements.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: How do we persuade more businesses and organisations to devote the time and precious resources to obtain these objectives together with us?

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: Upskilling our workforce to ensure that they have the necessary credentials and knowledge may get them past the door, but it is no guarantee that businesses and organisations will employ and train workers in the way that will build on and optimise their AI capabilities.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: In fact, we already have, within our system, the ability for the Government, unions and employers to collaborate closely to achieve the long-term objective of ensuring that our workforce is effectively equipped with the knowledge, skills, deep understanding and practical application outcomes.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: Our tripartite model, where all three partners, having built trust, mutual respect and equal partnership over decades, working hand in hand through this new phase of AI adoption, will help us to ensure that our workers, our businesses and our economy can seize new opportunities and advance together.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: For example, it has been reported that AI movie production startups in China are supported with incentives and financial support.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: They are reported to have pioneered micro-dramas or vertical dramas that is a new entertainment format making waves globally.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Knowledge workers like PMEs are highly exposed to AI, unlike earlier waves of automation that mostly impacted the rank and file.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Many of our middle-income PMEs belong to a sandwiched or under-served group.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: They are expected to perform like the top but are less protected than the bottom and they face increased competition from foreign PMEs.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Mid-career PMEs are sandwiched between younger and older dependents, and cannot afford to lose their jobs.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Yet they can take a longer time to find new jobs when displaced due to their higher income and age, often at the expense of a pay cut.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: We perceive PMEs as privileged and adaptable, who have resources and can take individual responsibility to upskill and also to cope with setbacks.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: AI is set to both augment and disrupt job tasks across all PME sectors at all levels.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: We must recognise AI as a transformative technology that has the potential to create new opportunities and shared prosperity but also the potential to widen inequality by concentrating wealth and power at the top, especially if guardrails are disregarded for the broad middle in the race to adopt AI.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: To this end, I submit that Singapore's approach to AI must be human-centred while AI-enabled growth must be worker-centred.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: This means that we commit to what I call the "3 Es”.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: The "3 Es" are equitable growth, enhanced protections and engaged workforce.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: When we talk about AI-driven jobless growth, this does not necessarily mean mass unemployment.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: However, it may mean that the gains from AI may not trickle down to the broad middle.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: This indicates that while we may not see jobless growth, we may well see growth with less jobs.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Jobseekers could be competing for fewer vacancies, underemployment could rise and wages could stagnate.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Young graduates may find more challenges securing full-time employment compared to before.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Globally, we have already seen a wave of companies, especially those in the tech sector, announce wide-ranging job cuts citing AI as a cause.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Equitable growth means that gains from AI-enabled growth will be shared with workers, in the form of better wages, welfare and work prospects.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: As Singapore aims to attract the world's top AI talent to our shores, we must also ensure this builds up and strengthens our Singaporean Core.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: I ask that the Government encourage reciprocity through programmes, like the Capability Transfer Programme, so that knowledge and expertise flow to our local PMEs.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: At the same time, the Government can also invest in homegrown AI talent by sending them on training stints to top AI companies overseas through programmes like the Overseas Market Immersion Programme.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Bringing in global expertise and developing our own global talent pipeline are two sides of the same coin.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Both deepen the capabilities of our local workforce.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Inevitably, some workers will be impacted in the transition to AI.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: We cannot leave them to sink or survive on their own.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: They will need career guidance, financial support and grace to bounce back stronger.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: By the same token, the Government can also consider allowing those with HDB housing loans a temporary deferment for up to six months, especially if they are unable to meet the mortgage payments to ease immediate cashflow needs.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Singapore has taken a considered, framework-based approach to AI governance.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Through IMDA's Model AI Governance Framework, the Cyber Security Agency’s addendum to secure agentic AI systems and voluntary testing toolkits, we have encouraged innovation and responsible adoption.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: But as AI moves from assisting decisions to making them, including in hiring, promotion and restructuring, we must keep pace.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Other advanced economies have already taken the lead to explicitly classify employment-related AI as "high risk".

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Will recruitment AI automatically rank candidates with disabilities lower?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: If HR relies on an AI tool to shortlist who stays and who goes during restructuring, what recourse does a worker have if the outcome feels unfair?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Who is accountable in this case – the HR team, the employer who procured the AI tool or the developer who built it?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: We are fortunate to have passed the Workplace Fairness Act.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Its principles – that employment decisions must be fair and merit-based and that every worker deserves fair access to good jobs – should apply regardless of whether those decisions are made by a human or by an algorithm.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: But while these principles are technology-agnostic, our current anti-discrimination levers have yet to explicitly address how they interact with AI-mediated decisions.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: As AI adoption accelerates, employers need clarity on what responsible use looks like, and workers need assurance that existing protections travel with them into an AI-enabled workplace.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: We should close this gap, not with regulations that stifles innovation but with clear, practical tripartite guidelines to ensure the just and fair transition.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Singapore's strength is our tripartite approach and we should leverage it.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: To that end, I ask that the Government consider the following.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Officers involved in data governance and cybersecurity can also update their skills and knowledge in this evolving area as more companies adopt AI that is integrated with enterprise data.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: The International Labour Organization has started this journey and Singapore, with our tripartite DNA, can be a frontrunner in this space.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Workers master AI and figure out how to embed AI into their workflows, not the other way round.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Ultimately, an organisation cannot be run by no workers and AI alone.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Simply imposing AI from the top will not produce results and can even create resistance and sunk cost.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Workers are end-users and experts in their own workflows.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: They know where AI adds value and where it falls short.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: If you want AI to work, you have to ask the people who do the work.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: We already have a proven mechanism for doing exactly this – our NTUC's CTCs.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: CTCs bring management, unions and workers together at the company level to co-design transformation plans, pairing technology adoption with job redesign, skills upgrading and better wages.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Senior Enrolled Nurse Lilian Teng, 69 years old, who has worked at TTSH for the past 19 years, put it simply: with technology making work less physically demanding, she can continue working effectively for as long as she remains healthy.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: That is what an engaged workforce looks like.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: But company-level efforts alone will not be enough.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: With the formation of the Tripartite Jobs Council, the Government, employers and unions can now coordinate sectoral transformation with workers at the centre, ensuring that AI training, job redesign and transition support are shaped by those on the ground, not just decided from the top.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Critically, the Tripartite Jobs Council can level up the CTC ecosystem to extend its reach beyond large employers to SMEs that may not have the resources to navigate their transformation alone.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: The Tripartite Jobs Council will do it at the national level.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Together, they ensure that AI transition is not something done to our workers, but with them.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: (In Mandarin):   Mr Deputy Speaker, AI is here – and it has arrived fast and with force.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: But we must ask: when AI generates wealth, whose pockets does it go into?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: AI creates wealth, but that wealth cannot flow only to employers.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Workers help bake the cake and they deserve a slice of it too.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Second, if jobs are lost, we cannot leave people to fend for themselves.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: We must put up the umbrella before the rain comes – prepare for the storm before it arrives.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: The AI transition cannot be decided by employers alone.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: As the saying goes, three cobblers together are better than a Zhuge Liang.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: The tripartite partners, unions and employers must work together, only then can we go far, steady and fast.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Share the cake fairly and walk forward together.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: That is the AI future that belongs to every Singaporean – one that puts people at its heart.
In English): To conclude, there has been much said about AI as a double-edged sword.
This metaphor has been used ad nauseam, but this is not untrue.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: There is genuine concern across the House about what AI will mean for our workers.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: We cannot slow down the development of AI.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: But we will not leave its outcomes to chance.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: We will work hard to secure a different deal between the companies that prosper here and the workers whose effort makes that prosperity possible.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: Not just in words, but in how jobs are designed, how people are trained and how gains are shared.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: In my conversations and engagements across the Ministry of Digital Development and Information (MDDI) and MOE work and through the Economic Strategy Review, the same concerns come up again and again.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: Will my job exist in five years' time?

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: Will AI widen inequality and leave the vulnerable behind?

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: If AI makes companies more productive, will workers share in the gains?

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: They come from people who have worked hard, built up skills and experience over time, and now sense that the ground is shifting beneath them.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: I will take each of these questions in turn.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: First, on whether today's jobs will continue to exist.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: Roles built primarily around repeating the same steps are the most exposed.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: This is not a verdict on the value of the people who do that work.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: It is a signal to us in government and to employers that we need to act now and not after the disruption arrives.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: But AI is more than just a technological advancement that replaces jobs.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: At the same time, it is opening up entirely new ways of working and new kinds of roles that did not exist before.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: Some academics have described AI as an "invention of a method of invention".

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: It expands the space of problems that can be solved, the products that can be built and industries that we can create.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: A small biotech team in Singapore can run experiments that would have required a national lab decades ago.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: A solo founder can ship software that took a hundred-man firm to deliver three years ago.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: So, competition sharpens, but the frontier also moves outward.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: That is why the Economic Strategy Review Committee that Senior Parliamentary Secretary Goh Hanyan and I co-chaired, focused on identifying new areas where Singapore can use AI to build a real competitive edge.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: And the Prime Minister's National AI Council will take this forward.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: Members have pointed out the impact of AI on PMEs, as AI automates routine and analytical tasks.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: The Economic Strategy Review team recognised this, which is why helping businesses and workers proactively navigate the transition was the focus of the committee chaired by Minister of State Goh Pei Ming and Minister of State Desmond Choo.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: For displaced workers, the committee studied how the Government, employers and unions could offer more timely help.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: As mentioned in our mid-term update, the Economic Strategy Review is studying ways to encourage earlier retrenchment notifications as raised by Mr Ng Chee Meng.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: For workers at risk of displacement, the Economic Strategy Review will recommend practical ways to help them move into more resilient roles with stronger demand.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: We will identify sectors with sustained labour demand and lower AI displacement risk, and we will work with unions and employers in those sectors to create clear, supported entry points for workers making the transition.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: We must make these pathways walkable and not just visible.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: To illustrate, a mid-career worker in a routine administrative role, for example in data entry or customer service, could be worried about AI displacing him.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: With job facilitation and reskilling support, the worker should be able to move into a sector where there are roles that build on his existing skillsets.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: For example, the worker could explore adjacent roles in healthcare administration.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: This is where we are seeing robust demand given the growth of our population healthcare needs, and healthcare requires uniquely human skills that are more resilient to disruption.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: It requires employers, unions, training providers and placement support working closely together, so that workers do not fall through the cracks during transition.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: No government in the world has all the answers to this transition and I would be wary of any that claims otherwise.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: What we in Singapore can commit to is this: we will not wait for perfect solutions before acting.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: We are starting now and we will adjust our efforts along the way.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: Technologies that amplify capability can also amplify gaps between those who adapt quickly and those who struggle to keep up.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: As Mr Mark Lee points out, some risks we face are that productivity gains accrue more to those already ahead, while the bottom of the career ladder may face erosion.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: This means starting earlier: building AI literacy into our schools, so that all students develop confidence with AI and not just those who have access to resources.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: Currently, every ITE and polytechnic student is already taught AI literacy as part of their course, and we are now bringing AI literacy and safe AI tools into primary and secondary school classrooms.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: This means that all students, regardless of economic background can learn about AI safely.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: They can also learn how AI can benefit their learning, such as to help them refine their ideas, and they also learn when they should not use AI.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: As Minister Desmond also pointed out earlier today, we are committed to supporting students who may not have strong family or parental supervision and support.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: While AI literacy in school will give them a good and strong foundation, we must continue to develop partnerships with the community and the self-help groups to make sure the supervision and support continue outside of school.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: We will track take-up and usage to see if we need to do more.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: Every Singaporean, regardless of starting point, should have the chance to experiment with AI tools and to build fluency.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: The third question is the hardest and the most important.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: We should be clear: this does not happen automatically.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: Left on its own, technology can lead to very uneven outcomes.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: That is why this is not just a market question.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: It is a question of how we shape norms and expectations in our economy.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: So, let me set out clearly what we expect.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: Companies that benefit from AI should invest in their people, not just in technology.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: That means training as many existing workers as possible and not just hiring new ones.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: It means facilitating their employees' access to frontier AI tools, creating communities of practice and incentivising learning and upskilling.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: We are not just asking our companies to do national service.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: We are asking them to do what is in their own long-term interest.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: In an AI age, human instinct and intuition will remain key.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: We all know that when we work with AI, we need to steer it.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: Ask the right questions and apply judgement as we refine the output iteratively.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: If you do not develop people who understand the context of your organisation and use this knowledge to reinforce your AI systems, you will be left with a very shallow and hollow company in future.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: If companies here replace humans completely with AI, they will find themselves, in future, to have no competitive edge, when AI is available to all companies.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: They will also find themselves at the mercies of AI companies.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: So, what we are working towards, is an approach that best positions our companies for sustainable growth in the long term.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: Mr Saktiandi Supaat brought up the need for balanced regulatory approaches that do not disincentivise AI adoption.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: Indeed, we will not seek to legislate our way to good outcomes.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: But we are equally clear that "voluntary" cannot mean "optional in practice".

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: Where public resources are deployed, we will ask for worker outcomes.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: We will work with companies to meet these expectations.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: Where there are persistent gaps, we will review how our support is applied.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: We will discuss with our tripartite partners on how this can be done fairly and effectively, in a way that incentivises companies to invest in training, job redesign, redeployment and placement.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: If we do this well, we will be able to create and sustain good jobs in the AI age.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: A good job is not just a job that exists.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: It is one that allows a worker to progress.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: It should pay fairly and reflect the productivity gains that technology brings.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: It should build skills that remain relevant, including as part of routine on-the-job training, so that workers are not stuck doing tasks that are easily replaced by automation.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: And it should give workers a sense of dignity and agency, not reduce their role to simply following instructions generated by machines.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: We have seen that when there is strong commitment, this is possible.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: At PSA, AI and automation have helped deliver record cargo volumes.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: And they continue to hire thousands more, because they are growing faster than the competition.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: To Mr Andre Low, I would say: automation and augmentation are not mutually exclusive.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: Protecting a worker can mean being intentional about automating tasks that are repetitive and physically demanding and upgrading the skills of the same worker so that technology can augment his capabilities as he takes on a higher value role.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: In the past, a customer wishing to trade in jewellery would interface with a sales advisor, who would pass on their case to a valuer to assess the authenticity of the jewellery.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: Now, these sales advisors can complement the existing pool of valuers, relieving their workload and reducing the customer wait times.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: This is the kind of responsible transformation we want to see in Singapore as the norm, not as the exception.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: We may differ on specific policy ideas or on how particular measures should be designed, funded or sequenced.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: This should not be a matter of party or ideology.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: It is a principle that we must uphold together as Singaporeans.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: If Singapore succeeds with our AI ambitions – and we should never assume success is automatic, because it will require sustained effort, difficult choices, adaptation and perhaps, some good fortune too.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: But if we succeed, then the Government will ensure that the benefits are widely shared.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: They must translate into better wages, better opportunities and greater security for all Singaporeans.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: The best protection for workers is not only redistribution after disruption.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: It is shaping how gains are created and shared from the outset and ensuring that Singaporean workers retain agency within an AI economy.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: This Government has been able to deliver these outcomes over decades of Singapore's development.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: And we are determined to continue doing so, as we navigate this AI transition.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: We have continuously adapted, refreshed and strengthened them as circumstances changed.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: Ultimately, every Singaporean should be able to look at what Singapore has built and say, "I have a stake in this progress.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: This future, belongs to me and my family too." This shared commitment is also what makes Singapore's approach to this transition distinctive.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: It is the way we work together, across Government, businesses and unions.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: Our commitment made in this House today is our commitment to you.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: To our business leaders: AI gives you powerful new capabilities.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: But how you use them will define your company's future, and your relationship with the people who built it alongside you.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: The companies that will lead in 10 years are not those that stripped costs the fastest, but those that built stronger teams by combining human judgement with machine capability.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: But I want to be clear about something else as well.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: There is real value in things that are fully human created, and that value may grow, not shrink, as AI becomes more prevalent.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: When everything around us is auto-generated, optimised and scaled, the things that are not will stand out.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: The live performance and encore that cannot be repeated.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: The hand-thrown ceramic bowl that carries the mark of a human hand.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: The meal prepared with care and craft, not just consistency.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: The conversation with the calligraphy master who has spent a lifetime honing his art.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: I think we will see a revival of appreciation for these things.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: And Singapore should not just acknowledge this, we should embrace it.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: Our artisans, our performers, our craftsmen are not swimming against the tide of AI.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: In a world saturated with AI-generated content, they may find themselves exactly where the world is looking.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: Beyond the near-term transition, there is a longer-term question we must answer.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: What do we need to do now with our education system, to prepare our students for the future world?

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: We must accept that AI will continue to get better at the tasks which machines do well.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: All the more, we need to focus on what makes us distinctly human.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: The curiosity that asks a question nobody has thought to ask.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: The creativity that connects ideas across domains in ways no training data predicts.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: The empathy that reads a room, earns trust and knows when the most efficient solution may not be the right solution.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: We must continue to build strong foundations and make sure our students do not become overly reliant on AI shortcuts.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: Our human brains are muscles that require exercise, and genuine mastery – the kind that holds up under pressure and that AI cannot simply replace – comes from hard work, from practice and from deep understanding.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: So, it was good to hear Ms Eileen Chong agree with this and we thank her for supporting our approach.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: The student who has truly mastered something is precisely the one with the confidence to venture beyond it.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: He will ask harder questions, take on problems without the obvious answers and he will develop interests that are genuinely his own.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: What we are building towards is an education system that demands both the discipline to go deep and the freedom to go wide.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: Not just because our students deserve both, but because Singapore's future depends on both.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: It will mean expanding what we count as excellence.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: Because if we get this right, if we develop a generation that is not just AI-literate but deeply human, then Singapore will not just survive this transition.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: We will be the kind of society that the next era of human progress is built around.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: But I want to end where I believe our attention must ultimately rest – on the generation we are building.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Today, I want to continue to support our senior workers and reflect their concerns in the age of AI.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: After leaving her previous job of more than 20 years, she found that the job search process had changed quite dramatically.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Resumes used to be written for people, but she found out that today, they are often screened by machines first.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Job applications also moved to digital portals that are not so intuitive for people like her to navigate.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: And for many of our senior workers, their experiences are shaped by three key gaps that I think we collectively must try to address.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: While Singapore has made progress in closing the access gap for seniors, smartphone ownership among them still lags behind other age groups.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: In addition, seniors may have less access to AI tools.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: I saw this first-hand at one of the AI workshops organised by my union SISEU for about 90 union leaders whose median age was about 53.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: While all of them used smartphones, many were trying AI tools for the first time.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: But with simple, guided use cases, they quickly picked it up and were using AI to generate posters for the union's Family Day and membership campaign.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Some even went to the extent to do banners for their families for birthdays and anniversaries.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: As we ended the session, many leaders came forward to share with me that they enjoyed the session and now, they realise that it is not so difficult to learn to use AI tools.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: The only thing they asked for is that they wished the session could be longer and the font on the slides can be bigger for them.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: It is easy to tell seniors to go and upskill, to go and take a course and reskill, but in reality, we know that with commitments, with bills to pay, with limited time and energy, taking the first step sometimes is not easy.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Many of them, we must remember, have lived through repeated cycles of change and transformation, and may feel fatigued, uncertain or even question the relevance of more training.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: We must make training more accessible for them at a suitable pace, through practical and bite-sized modules, and make AI more relevant to their job skills.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Even when senior workers are willing to learn, they may not have the same opportunities to benefit from AI in their actual jobs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: This is why we need to work with employers to give our seniors the opportunity to use AI tools and to reap productivity gains in their job.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Senior workers bring valuable experience and with AI, these strengths can go even further.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: I have spoken about this no less than two times in this Chamber.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Research from the Stanford Digital Economy Lab supports this.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: It highlighted that senior employment in the US has remained resilient and may even have grown with the introduction of AI because they see that seniors bring tacit experience, knowledge and soft skills that enable them to increase productivity with AI.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: To our senior workers, we understand your challenges and we are with you in this transition.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Start a course, try a tool, learn from those around you and you can thrive in the AI economy.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: It emphasises that growth must be anchored in fairness, resilience and opportunity for all and resolves to equip workers to seize these new opportunities.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: That must also apply to our senior workers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: NTUC recognises that long-lasting impact is best achieved through a partnership approach and has taken proactive steps through an AI-Ready SG initiative, which focuses on three key areas.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: First, training and upskilling workers to address skills and access gaps.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: To close the skills gap, NTUC LearningHub has developed a comprehensive AI learning pathway, with three different levels for learners with different proficiencies: foundational training to build AI literacy and fluency, intermediate training tailored to sectors or job roles, and advanced training for those in deep tech and who want to develop deeper AI specialisation and capabilities.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: I am glad to note that to date, there has been strong interest.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: This is something that the LearningHub has already been doing.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: For example, it works closely with companies to design AI courses aligned with the Government's skill frameworks and that are tailored to companies' needs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: We also partner with industry leaders such as AWS and Microsoft to certify learners' competencies based on industry demands.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: We will continue to expand this to more sectors and more industries.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: At the same time, under AI-Ready SG, we are also closing the access gap by providing union members with subsidies of up to 50% for AI premium subscription tools through NTUC's Union Training Assistance Programme (UTAP).

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: I think there are a total of 20 or 21 tools.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: We are offering this as part of membership privileges only because we are using the existing UTAP funding model catered for our members' training.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: But we will continue to review this, depending on the take-up and the interest over time.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: We are also partnering sector agencies like the Civil Aviation Authority of Singapore to develop sector AI training pathways for our union leaders.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Second, we are supporting firms in business transformation and job redesign through NTUC's CTCs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: I know you have heard many examples over the course of this debate.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: It is from the Evergreen Group, a local office and stationary supplier.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Through a CTC Grant project with the Singapore Manual and Mercantile Workers' Union (SMMWU), it implemented an AI-powered e-ordering system to automate the ordering process and improve inventory management.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Workers could focus on higher-value tasks such as managing customer relationships and using data to optimise inventory.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: This is what we mean by win-win outcomes – where businesses become more productive and our workers progress with them.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Third, we are improving job matching with new products and services to help workers access good jobs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Through close support from her e2i career coach, she gained a deeper understanding of her skills and the new job market.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Her coach also introduced her to NTUC's AI Career Coach and e2i's AI Interviewer.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: With support and encouragement, Mdm Foo could confidently use these AI tools to sharpen her resume and also practise her interviews before the actual session.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: I am glad to share that Mdm Foo has found a new role and has gained familiarity with AI in the process.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: It supports workers to build AI skills, gives them access to tools to apply these skills and works with businesses to improve productivity and create new opportunities.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Looking ahead, we welcome companies and partners to come onboard as we scale our efforts and increase our reach to ultimately deliver better support for our businesses and for our workers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: But the scale of change brought about by AI is also significant, with great uncertainty and anxiety among workers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: This is why tripartism, with its proven track record built over many decades of open communication and trust, is critical to this challenge.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: In the 1980s, when computers first entered the workplace, workers were concerned that these machines could replace their roles in data entry and filing and companies were anxious about costs, skills shortage and disruptions to their daily operations.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: The Government invested in infrastructure and skills, including the National Computer Board, to drive nationwide adoption of IT.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Employers stepped forward to transform their businesses with new technologies and redesigned workflows.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: The Labour Movement drove skills upgrading en-masse, organised workshops and seminars, preparing workers mentally and practically for change.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: The Tripartite Jobs Council will take on a practical and iterative approach.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: We may not have all the answers upfront, but we are clear that our deep trust built over decades of cooperation and shared goals will allow us to achieve our aspiration of inclusive economic progress.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: (In Mandarin):   Mr Deputy Speaker, Singapore needs to harness AI to drive the next phase of economic growth.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: But more importantly, this growth must be built on a foundation of fairness, inclusivity and resilience for all.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Singapore's tripartite partners – unions, employers, and the Government – have worked closely together over many years, building deep trust that has allowed us to unite and overcome challenges together, no matter what difficulties we face.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: We will continue to support our workers in seizing opportunities and strengthening their competitiveness in the age of AI.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: This initiative helps them bridge the gaps in awareness, skills and access, so that they are better prepared for the AI-driven economy.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: As the saying goes, "Opportunity favours the prepared and success belongs to the most persistent." The age of AI is already upon us.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: I hope that everyone will join NTUC in actively upskilling, learning and applying AI. : Mr Deputy Speaker, AI is the defining technology of our generation.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: But we face this challenge with strong foundations built over decades of tripartite cooperation.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: To our tripartite partners, let us continue working closely together to help our firms transform and stay competitive, while supporting our workers to remain productive and to maximise opportunities.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: To our workers, we will continue to support you to leverage AI.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: And to our senior workers, your experience matters and it is my firm belief that it will be an advantage in the AI era.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Closer to home, Members of this House have spoken about something that weighs on the minds of all of our fellow Singaporeans: the anxiety that AI may erode our skills, our experience built up over years or even take over our jobs.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: This anxiety has been sharpened by news of large tech firms announcing lay-offs attributed to AI adoption.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: These are legitimate concerns and we take it seriously.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: And a change of this magnitude is indeed unsettling.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: But AI can and will create opportunities that we cannot yet fully imagine.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Of course, it will, at the same time, also bring about disruptions that we cannot fully foresee.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: But there are, at the same time, early signs that gives us reason for cautious optimism.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Because they found that AI could handle the predictable and the routine, but customers still wanted human judgement, empathy and the genuine connection that AI could not provide.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: But one thing it could not appreciate was the impact and the anxiety that many, many workers feel.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: It could not offer empathy, it could not empathise, it could not understand nuance, nor could it generate policy responses that capture the essence of what workers are really experiencing.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: And this is what no algorithm can replace.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: In Parliament, we are also adopting and embracing AI as we equip our staff on this journey.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I see a few hands being put up.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Please raise your hands again, those who wish to seek clarifications.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre
text: I have clarifications for the Minister of State Lau and Minister Tan.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre
text: My clarification for Minister of State Jasmin Lau is, I am glad to hear that she has put to me that automation and augmentation are not mutually exclusive.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre
text: She went on to define that as being intentional about automating repetitive and physical tasks and upgrading the skills of that same worker.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre
text: So, I am glad to hear that because that is exactly how I have defined augmentation in my speech.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre
text: And she also noted that I use the term automation in my speech as a shorthand for scenarios where a job is entirely fully automated away at the expense of the worker.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre
text: To Minister Tan, he suggested that proposals by my colleague, Mr Gerald Giam and myself, are anchored on the premise that Singaporeans are hapless passengers along for the ride on this AI journey.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre
text: I would urge the Minister to clarify how he has managed to read that basis into our speeches.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre
text: And secondly, I would simply use the language of Minister of State Lau as well, that we do not believe that strong social safety nets, and upskilling Singaporeans and urging them to embrace AI are mutually exclusive.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre
text: In fact, we believe that strong social safety nets are precisely what will enable Singaporeans to take a risk-taking approach and embrace the opportunities that AI will deliver.

speaker: Ms Jasmin Lau
text: Very glad to hear that we are on the same page.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Likewise, I am really glad, particularly from Mr Low that, and I presume, since he is mentioning his name, Mr Giam as well, that they believe that Singaporeans have what it takes to work with the Government, with the unions, with the businesses to chart their own future.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: So, I thank the Member for that affirmation.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: My response to the Minister, yes, I definitely believe Singaporeans have the ability to chart this future for themselves.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: But the Minister has offered a choice of two visions in his response to my speech; and I thank him for reading it carefully.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: But I do not agree with his characterisation of my proposal as a resignation to displacement.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: It is about providing the security required for assurance and success.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: And I would like to remind him that the proposal I put forward has actually got two limbs.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: The first provides a direct stake in our prosperity.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: The second, which utilises nearly half the fund, is a direct investment in the skills and competencies of our workers.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: It provides a wage support and technical expertise that companies, especially SMEs, need to conduct on-the-job (OJT) training that is fully relevant to their workers.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: And earlier, Minister of State Jasmin Lau said gains from AI must translate into greater security for all Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: Specifically, what is the Government's plan to move from discretionary spending to a structural sharing of AI wealth to protect the economic agency of our workers?

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: I think the straight answer is through real income improvement.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: That is how we envisage the pie to be shared.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat
text: First, why does he believe that the SkillsFuture course enrolment is a reliable proxy for seriousness?

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat
text: I have some of my residents who have gone for some of these AI courses; they are not very complimentary on the content of these courses.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat
text: So, there is a perception that some of the quality of these courses is not as good as it could be.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat
text: And second, does the Minister not think that universal supply of frontier agentic tools will create its own demand eventually?

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
